Love Eva Mendes and Ryan Gosling’s Mini Christmas Trees? Here’s How To Make Your Own

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (913 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that eva Mendes and Ryan Gosling are one of those celebrity couples that keep their heads down and their private lives just that; private.
  • Now, we usually think of a Christmas tree as being larger than life, and twice, especially when it's in the home of a celebrity.
  • Eva and Ryan have opted for a similarly unfussy approach; the couple's kitchen island is full of miniature Christmas trees.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that eva Mendes and Ryan Gosling are one of those celebrity couples that keep their heads down and their private lives just that; private. So sue us, then, that we get excited when they offer us a sneak-peek into their world... especially when it comes with a Christmassy twist!

Now, we usually think of a Christmas tree as being larger than life, and twice, especially when it's in the home of a celebrity. Honestly, though, most stars seem to be taking a laidback approach to their festive decor of late, whether it's the Beckhams' bow-filled Christmas tree, Sarah Jessica Parker's floral Christmas tree, or even Michelle Obama's twig tree.

Eva and Ryan have opted for a similarly unfussy approach; the couple's kitchen island is full of miniature Christmas trees. Check it out:.

A post shared by Eva Mendes (@evamendes).

In a recent development, and just like that, they've proven you don’t need a large traditional evergreen tree to make your house look stylish during the holidays. In fact, if you decide to follow in Eva Mendes and Ryan Gosling's footsteps, you might not need to buy much at all.

All you have to do is take a simple stroll around your garden with a pair of pruners and a small pot to get the same look; fortunately, some experts told me exactly how to do it.

“The best mini Christmas trees start with a walk around your own garden,” states Nick Alan, founder of Palma Botanical Co., who has been growing plants for 25 years.

Sources indicate that his picks? “Conifer tips like cedar, cypress, juniper and fir hold their needles longest. Boxwood and rosemary fill gaps and add scent.”.

For clean cuts, Nick Alan recommends these Fiskars SoftGrip bypass pruners.

In a recent development, use gentle hands with the shrub, though. “Harvest on a cool morning with clean pruners, cutting just above a side shoot so the plant regrows, and take no more than a third of any shrub,” states Alan.

Nadi Melam, founder of Florals Memories, has a simple pot method for getting the Eva Mendes and Ryan Gosling look this Christmas.

“Fill a 4-inch pot with damp sand (this will help hold your stems upright and will allow you to leave the tree in its pot as it dries). Remove the needles from the bottom 2 inches of each stem (you don’t want any foliage to rot in the sand!).”.

It has been revealed that once this is done, she states you should “arrange the stems from tallest in the middle to shortest as you work your way out (creating a cone shape).” Remember, though, that cut foliage won’t last forever. “Mist every few days and keep it away from the stove, dishwasher vent, and sunny windows. Expect two to three weeks, swapping tired sprigs,” says Alan.

A living tree means you don’t have the extra work of worrying about sprigs. “For a kitchen island display like Eva Mendes and Ryan Gosling's, I like a living miniature tree best, because it does two jobs at once: it looks festive, and it stays useful after Christmas,” says Morgan Brooks, founder and editor of Plant Style Home.

Brooks states rosemary is the practical pick for a kitchen: “Rosemary is the most practical in a kitchen because you can pick sprigs for cooking, and it smells wonderful near the stove.”.

For care, Brooks says: “I keep young trees in cool spots away from radiators and water the compost so it stays lightly damp but never wet.” Alan adds: “Give it your brightest window, water when the top inch is dry, and plant it out afterward in zone 8 and warmer.”.

Shop Live Rosemary Christmas Trees:.

Your kitchen island may be a great spot for trees, but don’t forget it’s also a workspace for cooking. Keep your trees all to one side and never let them near heat sources, especially the dry foliage.

Roberta Sabbatini, founder of ItalianTouch Events, states that “a little greenery with one beautiful ribbon often looks more considered than a crowded arrangement.”.

For the layout, Melam indicates: “I love displaying mini trees in odd-numbered clusters of varying heights. Negative space is key! I’d keep the tallest stem 10-12 inches so as not to compete with faucets, etc.”.

A tray helps too: “Displaying them on a tray or wooden slab can help tie them together & unify the display (as opposed to them looking like random pots on a counter).” On a budget, Alan notes: “Pine cones, dried orange slices and ribbon dress them cheaply.”.

Alan has one note of advice for people with pets or small children: “Skip holly, yew and mistletoe around pets and kids, since all are toxic.”.

While Eva Mendes and Ryan Gosling have both played a variety of characters throughout their film careers, we really do think that “people with a stunning Christmas kitchen island” is one we really fancy having a go at, too.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that while many of our gardens are settling in for winter, Ezeiza, Argentina, is enjoying the last stretch of spring before summer arrives in December. Today we’re heading back to visit Ezequiel. We’ve followed his cottage garden through the seasons over the years, including another beautiful spring visit. After some difficult weather, he is back with another patch as his garden fills with flowers ahead of summer.

I hope you are all doing very well during the autumn in the North. In my country, following the harsh and troublesome “El Niño” weather phenomenon, the long-awaited and much-loved spring has finally arrived in my cottage garden in Ezeiza.

Sources indicate that plants and flowers are just beginning to emerge, a promise of the summer that will be in full swing by December here in the Southern Hemisphere. Penstemons, salvias, irises, verbenas, dahlias, bulbines, daisies, and my lemon tree… Everything has begun to stir, grow, and grace us with beautiful blossoms, lovely scents, and fragrances.

Thank you, as always, for being there! And thank you for sharing in the joy of my garden.

From Argentina, sending you my best regards and a major hug.

A look into Ezequiel’s cottage garden in Ezeiza, Argentina.

‘Hot Lips’ salvia (Salvia microphylla ‘Hot Lips’, Zones 7–10) in bloom.

Louisiana iris (Iris × louisiana, Zones 4–9) showing off.

A view of the backyard perennial beds.

It has been revealed that purple coneflowers (Echinacea purpurea, Zones 3–9) are flowering next to the large sweep of lavender (Lavandula cvs., Zones 5–10) along the side of the driveway. I can practically smell the lavender looking at this photo!

This massive lantana (Lantana camara, Zones 8–11) stopped me in my tracks! Here in the North, we usually grow lantana as an annual because it isn’t winter hardy. Seeing what this tender perennial can become in a warmer climate is pretty incredible.

Bearded iris (Iris cvs., Zones 3–9), California poppy (Eschscholzia californica, Zones 8–10), and orange bulbine (Bulbine frutescens, Zones 9–11) make a colorful combination in this perennial bed.

Another view of the massive lantana, this time with a gorgeous specimen crimson bottlebrush (Callistemon citrinus, Zones 8–11) in full bloom.

Another view of the backyard. This photo has me wondering just how far it extends. I’m so curious about the layout of this garden—it seems like there’s something fresh to discover just about everywhere!

According to recent reports, thank you for bringing us back to your beautiful garden, Ezequiel! It’s always such a treat to see what’s growing in your corner of the world, especially while our seasons here in the North are moving in the opposite direction.

#102182. Don't Buy a Poinsettia Until You've Checked This Tiny Detail – It Reveals How Long It Will Last

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1161 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Gardeningknowhow ↗ Open Full Page

Don't Buy a Poinsettia Until You've Checked This Tiny Detail – It Reveals How Long It Will Last

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1161 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that it happens every December.
  • In a recent development, some of that can be blamed on poinsettia care after you get home, like a cold windowsill or a pot left sitting in water.
  • Industry observers note that there's an easy way to tell a fresh one from a tired one, and hardly anybody looks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that it happens every December. You bring home a full, bright red poinsettia, set it on the table, and a week or two later the colorful bracts start to curl and fall. By Christmas morning, the plant looks tired and half bare.

In a recent development, some of that can be blamed on poinsettia care after you get home, like a cold windowsill or a pot left sitting in water. Much of it starts at the store, though. The plant was already on its way out before it ever went in the cart.

Industry observers note that there's an easy way to tell a fresh one from a tired one, and hardly anybody looks. Forget the red for a second. Down in the center of each cluster of colored leaves are some tiny yellow-green buds, and those say a lot more about how long the color will hold up. It's kind of a strange thing to judge a plant by, but trust the process.

Sources indicate that those colorful "petals" on a poinsettia aren't petals at all. They're bracts, and they color up in fall as the nights get longer. Right in the middle sit the real flowers, small knobby clusters called cyathia. Each one is a little cup holding a single female flower and several male flowers, often with a yellow gland on its rim.

Industry observers note that cyathia go through the same cycle on every plant. They start out tight and green or red-tipped, open to shed yellow pollen, and then drop off. After the cyathia fall, the colored bracts usually follow before long.

It has been revealed that some of the newer poinsettia varieties hang on to their cyathia longer. So it isn't a sure thing, but it's still one of the better clues you get in the store. Any color works for this check, whether you're eyeing red or the pink poinsettias at Walmart (which come in a four-pack for maximum festive joy).

In a recent development, bend down and look closely at the center of a few bracts. Plants on the same table can be at different stages, so check more than one. Ideally, the cyathia are mostly closed, green or tipped with red, and fresh-looking. Some yellow showing is fine on its own. That's often just the gland on the side of the cup – it doesn't mean the flower has opened.

In a recent development, now compare that to a plant where the buds have split open and yellow pollen is dusting the bracts below them. If you see that, or you find bare stubs where cyathia used to be, that poinsettia has been blooming a while already. It may look fine today, but it has less time left than the one beside it with tight buds.

Classic red poinsettias come in a four-pack from Costa Farms, and you can order them on Amazon – and the same quick look at the center works on a plant that demonstrates up at the door.

It has been revealed that the green leaves under the bracts deserve a look too. Check for yellow leaves low on the stems, or bare spots where leaves have already dropped. Cold, poor light, and watering trouble can all cause that. Pass on a plant that droops or looks wilted, along with any that have torn, bruised, or creased bracts. Bluish or whitish edges on the bracts can be a sign of cold injury.

According to recent reports, flip a few leaves over as well. Whiteflies, such as the silverleaf whitefly (Bemisia tabaci), are common on poinsettias, and a puff of tiny white insects lifting off when you brush the plant is a bad sign.

Recent findings suggest that lift the pot if you can. Soggy soil in a heavy pot may mean it's been sitting in water inside its foil, and roots kept that wet can rot. Pay attention to where the plants are displayed, too. Poinsettias crowded by the automatic doors can catch a blast of cold air every time the doors open, and plants left packed in plastic sleeves for days can droop and drop their flowers early – ethylene gas builds up inside the sleeve.

When you get home, use a soil moisture meter, like the Xlux moisture meter available on Amazon, to take the guesswork out of watering.

It has been revealed that the journey home is where poinsettias tend to get hurt. When it's below 50°F (10°C) outside, sleeve or wrap the plant before it leaves the store, even for the short walk to the car. Just a few minutes of cold air can damage the bracts and leaves, and the damage may not show right away. Save the garden center for your last stop so the plant isn't stuck in a cold car while you're in other stores, and warm the car up first. Once you're inside, get the sleeve off pretty rapidly.

Sources indicate that pick a bright room for your poinsettia. Keep the plant near a window but out of hard, direct sun, and well clear of heat vents, the fireplace, and any door that lets in a draft.

Recent findings suggest that normal house temperatures work fine, roughly 65 to 70°F (18 to 21°C) during the day, with nights around 60°F (16°C) or a little warmer. Window glass gets cold at night, though, and so can the air right beside it. Set a digital indoor thermometer, like the TempPro TP50, for a night or two, and you'll know for sure.

In a recent development, stick a finger in the pot before you water. If the top of the soil is dry, go ahead, and if it's still damp, wait a day or so. That shiny foil holds water like a bowl, so poke a few holes in the bottom, or take the pot out and water it over the sink until it drains. A ceramic planter, like this Garden & Home Red 8 Inch Indoor Ceramic Plant Pot, with drainage holes and saucer, is a much nicer option than foil anyway. You don't need fertilizer while a poinsettia is in bloom.

Industry observers note that pick a plant with tight little buds in the center, keep it somewhere warm and bright, and the color can hold for weeks after the holidays. So the next time you're standing in front of a whole table of red, skip past the brightest one for a second and look at the center first.

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success indicates that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

How to Use Ornamental Edibles for Eye-Catching Containers

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that if you’re looking past vegetables, fruits, and herbs because you think they only belong in the kitchen garden, you’re missing a whole range of interesting, versatile possibilities for creating exciting ornamental containers. Edible plants can bring striking foliage, flowers, fruit, and structure to a container, even when producing a harvest isn’t the primary goal.

As a designer, I create vignettes in my gardens that engage the senses. It’s no different when composing a container or a grouping of containers. For now, set aside flavor and look at their other sensory qualities: visual appeal, fragrance, texture, and even the sounds of foliage and seed heads moving in the wind.

Read More: Best Sensory Garden Plants for Sound, Touch, Taste & Smell.

Industry observers note that successful container design balances aesthetics with the growing needs of individual plants. Before exploring specific edimentals—plants valued for both their edible and ornamental qualities—consider a few practical guidelines.

Growing vegetables in containers demands certain conditions if you want a good harvest. But when appearance takes priority over production, you can make different choices. For instance, allowing lettuce and other leafy greens to bolt can introduce interesting flower stalks and seed heads, even though the leaves may become bitter and less desirable for eating.

Industry observers note that containers give you greater control over growing conditions, but plants still need the right light, moisture, and soil. Choose edible varieties that tend to be compact, dwarf, bush, or well-behaved vines or climbers.

Recent findings suggest that it’s helpful to choose the largest container your budget and space will allow. Larger pots generally provide more room for roots and retain moisture longer, while smaller containers dry out more swiftly and may require more frequent watering and feeding. Mixing container sizes also adds visual interest to a display. Whatever the size, make sure the container has adequate drainage.

One advantage of container gardening is the ability to tailor the soil to your plants’ needs. Start with a quality potting mix and choose plants with similar preferences for drainage, moisture, and soil acidity. This flexibility also lets you grow plants that might struggle in your native garden soil.

According to recent reports, because container plants depend on a limited volume of soil, they may need supplemental fertilizer as nutrients become depleted. Think about what you’re trying to encourage: Excess nitrogen, for example, can promote leafy growth at the expense of flowers or fruit. Choose a fertilizer appropriate for your plants, follow label directions, and consult your local nursery or Extension service for specific recommendations.

Mulch helps regulate soil temperature and retain moisture, even in containers. For open compositions where the soil surface is visible, use decorative materials such as small pine cones, shells, buckwheat hulls, or gravel. Leaf mold and finely shredded bark work well, too. Apply a shallow layer that allows water to pass through, and keep mulch away from plant crowns and stems.

In a recent development, use what you have and think about growing your own. Many vegetables are quite easy to start from seed. Growing your own is both economical and a way to reduce the need for purchased transplants, especially when you use peat-free soil mixes. Choosing peat-free mixes can also help reduce demand for peat extracted from carbon-storing wetlands. Collect rainwater where permitted for an additional irrigation source. Avoid using untreated household gray water on edible crops. Incorporating perennials also extends the life of your displays. They can be combined with seasonal plants or relocated elsewhere in the garden when a container needs refreshing.

It has been revealed that the ever-popular Thriller-Filler-Spiller container method holds its ground because of its snappy moniker and reliable formula. In this method, the thriller is the dramatic focal point; the filler is a bushy, mid-level plant or plants; and the spiller—wait for it—spills over the edge of the container. It’s an easy enough recipe that most people can create something attractive, but truthfully, many fail to think much about what they are combining, which results in the substantial-box special: a nondescript spiky grass towering over a showy fuchsia, with invasive creeping Jenny (Lysimachia nummularia, Zones 3–9) trailing out.

Sources indicate that we can do better. While perhaps less catchy, think about composing your container much like you might a landscape. Consider structure (the framework); form and habit (the shape); spatial orientation (how it reads visually—does the plant have a horizontal, vertical, or some other orientation?); visual texture (is the foliage fine, coarse, or medium?); and color (is it intense, receding, or something else?). Go beyond appearance and consider the full range of sensory experience: how plants move in the wind and what that sounds like, what they smell like, and how they feel when brushed up against.

According to recent reports, not every plant or combination will hit all the notes, so don’t stress. Focus on a few complementary qualities. Combine the plants in your container to create contrasts or enhance similarities. Look at leaf, bloom, and seed head form. The idea is to create layers—low, mid, and upper—and aim for three to five plants that play off each other’s traits within the container.

Are you trying to create something formal, informal, transitional, organic, or eclectic? Knowing how you want your container to read to the viewer can help you make choices about which edible plants may be a better addition to the mix.

In a recent development, when composing your containers, don’t forget to look beyond edimentals. Often the best containers mix edible plants with purely ornamental plants, such as leafy or flowering perennials and small shrubs. The juxtaposition of disparate plants usually determines a container’s success—different textures, colors, heights, and forms.

While incorporating disparate elements creates visual interest, it’s also key to give the eye somewhere to rest. A collection of pots filled with different plant combinations can feel jarring without repetition or quieter areas to balance the display.

A repeat may be exactly what it sounds like: using the same plant or using the same color, form, or texture across pots. Areas to pause are pots that may contain one uniform element—such as like plants, colors, or containers.

Another approach is to view the containers as individual components. Rather than composing containers with several different kinds of plants (including vegetables, of course), try grouping containers that each have one type of plant. This can be a powerful display akin to naturalistic block-style planting design.

In a recent development, sometimes a container needs more. Perhaps it needs some staking for a vine, or simply a bit of additional texture. Incorporate natural materials such as pruned branches (dry or living), fallen branches covered in lichen, wild berry clusters, pine cones, grape or hop vines, dried elements such as grasses, or even small stumps.

Sources indicate that and don’t neglect the value of seed heads—just because that kale bloom has now passed doesn’t necessarily mean you want to remove the plant; wait to see those prolific little yellow pods. And a radish gone to seed showcases its most redeeming feature: crunchy seed clusters that rattle in the wind!

By definition, a container is simply a receptacle for holding goods or objects, so feel free to think beyond the pots you find at the nursery. Salvaged and vintage items work well combined with more traditional terra-cotta pots. Take a high-low approach and use found items from your own home along with a special planter from a boutique garden center.

According to recent reports, don’t forget these irreverent options can also be repurposed in unexpected applications—that antique copper colander can go on to lead a new life as a hanging basket. Just make sure repurposed containers provide adequate drainage and are suitable for growing food if you initiative to harvest from them.

One of the biggest benefits of working with containers is the opportunity to modify them by adding or removing plants to capture the best seasonal foliage. While many edibles are annuals that end their season late in the year, others produce seed heads or even a second flush after cutback.

Some common edible members of the carrot family (Apiaceae), including carrots (Daucus carota, biennial); parsnips (Pastinaca sativa, biennial); parsley (Petroselinum crispum, biennial); and celery and celeriac (Apium graveolens, biennial), produce flowers in their second growing season. Their delicate foliage and umbrella-shaped flower clusters add texture and attract pollinators. Deep-rooted crops such as carrots and parsnips need sufficiently deep containers, particularly if you initiative to leave them in place for a second season.

Osage orange (Maclura pomifera, Zones 4–9) isn’t a citrus fruit at all. This North American native tree produces large, greenish yellow, orange-like fruits with a distinctive, bumpy surface. Although the fruits aren’t considered edible, their unusual appearance and citrus-like fragrance make them wonderful decorative accessories for autumn container displays.

Another lesser-known edible is a well-known perennial: ostrich fern (Matteuccia struthiopteris, Zones 2–8). Its tightly coiled young fronds, known as fiddleheads, are harvested as a spring delicacy before unfurling into the familiar feathery foliage.

Lady fern (Athyrium filix-femina, Zones 3–8) offers similarly beautiful emerging fronds for ornamental containers, but it should not be treated as an interchangeable edible. Many ferns contain potentially harmful compounds, so accurate identification is essential. Only properly identified ostrich fern fiddleheads should be eaten, and they must be thoroughly cooked. For more information, see the University of Maine Cooperative Extension’s guide to fiddlehead safety. Of course, you can simply enjoy their fascinating emerging foliage up close in a container.

Sources indicate that vegetables that you may not have thought about embracing in your ornamental containers include okra (Abelmoschus esculentus, annual), with its large pods and hibiscus-like flowers; artichokes, such as ‘Purple Italian Globe’ (Cynara cardunculus var. scolymus ‘Purple Italian Globe’, Zones 7–10), with dramatic silvery foliage and purple flower heads (use your largest container); cucamelon (Melothria scabra, annual), also called mouse melon, which resembles a tiny watermelon on a prolific climbing vine; and leafy greens of all sorts. Look out for the striking edible red-veined dock (Rumex sanguineus, Zones 5–8), with the unpalatable common name, bloody dock—it’s a stunner. Its green leaves are marked with vivid red veins, and the young foliage is edible in moderation, although it contains oxalic acid.

More common edibles with uncommon traits include delicate currant tomatoes such as ‘Sweet Pea’ (Solanum pimpinellifolium ‘Sweet Pea’, annual) or compact tomatoes such as ‘Tiny Tim’ (Solanum lycopersicum ‘Tiny Tim’, annual).

Alpine strawberries (Fragaria vesca, Zones 4–9) come in a range of colors from white and pale yellow to pink and red, depending on the selection. These diminutive berries add character and spill over the edge of containers.

Sources indicate that peppers such as the teardrop ‘Biquinho Red’ (Capsicum chinense ‘Biquinho Red’, annual) are eye-catching and tolerant of many conditions. Compact blueberry (Vaccinium cvs., Zones 3–8) foliage glows red in the autumn, acting as a foil for its partners.

In a recent development, and there are so. Many. More. Whatever you’re interested in, you can find an edimental that will fill that niche.

Edible plants offer a broader palette that many gardeners and designers overlook—choosing them for containers broadens your range of plant materials and, most importantly, creates opportunities for delight and intrigue when used in unexpected ways.

According to recent reports, they also make it possible to garden in small spaces or places where in-ground planting isn’t practical. Containers can be moved to improve growing conditions, rearranged to create a fresh focal point, or grouped to screen an unwanted view. They also let you accommodate plants that might struggle in your native soil or spread too aggressively in garden beds, such as mint (Mentha cvs., Zones 3–9) or sunchokes (Helianthus tuberosus, Zones 3–9). Just be sure to give vigorous plants enough room to grow.

In the eastern United States, ornamental kales and cabbages, paired with mums, are a common sight this time of year. While there is nothing inherently wrong with them, now you know you have more edimental options, so why not experiment with a wider range of edible plants? From colorful leafy greens to fruiting vines and impressive seed heads, there’s no shortage of possibilities for creating containers that look as interesting as the plants themselves.

Industry News: Think Winter Kills All the Wasps in Your Yard? Here's Where Next Year's Queens Are Hiding

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1121 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After the first hard frost, the wasps that pestered every picnic in August are suddenly gone.
  • Before you look up how to kill wasps next spring, know that yellowjackets, paper wasps, and hornets live in colonies that last just one season.
  • Some of the places where wasps hide in winter are right in your yard.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After the first hard frost, the wasps that pestered every picnic in August are suddenly gone. It's easy to figure the cold finished them off. So where do wasps go in winter, and do wasps die in winter at all? Most of them do – just not the ones that count for next year.

Before you look up how to kill wasps next spring, know that yellowjackets, paper wasps, and hornets live in colonies that last just one season. Each colony leaves behind young queens that have already mated and will ride out the cold on their own.

Some of the places where wasps hide in winter are right in your yard. Firewood, loose bark, and the gaps around a shed door can each hold a queen until spring.

Sources indicate that for the common social wasps, the colony only lasts a year. Each spring, a single queen starts a small nest and raises the first workers herself. The colony grows through summer, and by late summer it switches to raising males and newly introduced queens. The new queens mate in fall, then leave the nest for good.

Industry observers note that everyone else is left behind. By the time hard freezes settle in, the old queen, the workers, and the males have died, and the papery nest sits empty for good. The mated queens are the only ones that make it into winter, and they don't go back to the nest. Each one finds its own sheltered spot. Many still won't last until spring, but the ones that do will start the whole thing over.

Here are some of the common places you'll find queens hiding.

It has been revealed that rake back a deep drift of oak leaves in midwinter, and the ground underneath is often softer and less frozen than the open lawn. Yellowjacket queens may crawl into that leaf litter or under old mulch and pulled plants at the edge of a bed. They stay perfectly still. You'd likely never notice one. Some leaves left in place also help butterflies and moths overwinter, and there's no reason to rake every corner bare because of wasps.

Sources indicate that stacked firewood is full of narrow gaps out of the wind, and rotting logs and old stumps offer soft wood a queen can tuck into. Pull a few splits from the bottom of the stack in winter, and you may find one clinging to the bark, too cold to move much. Check each piece before carrying it inside – a warm living room can wake a dormant queen. Bring in only what you'll burn that day. Walmart's leather palm work gloves are tough enough for sorting through the stack.

Loose bark on a dead tree makes a snug pocket. Yellowjacket queens squeeze into those gaps. Birds have a hard time reaching them there, and the bark keeps off most of the weather. On a mild winter day, try lifting a slab of it off an old stump. You could find a queen pressed flat in the gap underneath, barely moving. Put the bark back if you do. She isn't going anywhere until spring.

According to recent reports, sheds, garages, and barns are full of cracks around door frames and window trim. Queens often move in during fall and stay put until spring. Paper wasps tend to seek out high spots for the winter, and they sometimes overwinter in clusters, packed together at the peak of a roof or along a rafter. To keep queens from slipping in next fall, cover open vents with stainless steel mesh, which Amazon sells in small sheets.

Queens find their way into wall voids and attics through gaps where siding meets trim, or through cracks around windows. Temperatures in there usually stay above freezing. Ever find a slow, groggy wasp on a window inside the house in January? It's usually a lone queen that wandered in from the walls, drawn toward the light. An active nest looks different – steady traffic in and out of the same hole in summer or early fall points to a live colony inside the wall.

Don't plug that hole while the nest is active, since the wasps may chew through to the inside. Once the colony has died off, seal exterior cracks with a flexible sealant such as DAP Dynaflex 230 from Home Depot.

According to recent reports, some yellowjacket queens spend the winter underground, but not in the nest they came from. That old nest is abandoned when the colony dies, and it isn't used again. She might use an empty mouse or vole burrow instead, a crack between rocks, or a small pocket in loose soil.

A home compost pile that hasn't been turned in a while is another possibility. If you turn the pile in winter, move slowly and wear gloves, and she'll probably stay put.

It has been revealed that usually, there's no need. Wasps are useful predators. Yellowjackets and paper wasps hunt caterpillars and other soft-bodied insects to feed their young, and the adults visit flowers for nectar, moving some pollen around as they go. A queen sleeping under a log at the back of the yard poses little risk, and next summer her colony will probably eat a good number of garden pests.

In a recent development, doors, windows, and play areas are a different story. Seal gaps around the house in late summer, before queens go looking for winter shelter, and check that window screens fit tightly. Home Depot carries a door jamb weatherstrip set that closes the gaps around exterior doors.

Once spring warms up, glance at the eaves and porch ceiling every so often. A brand-newly introduced nest is about the size of a golf ball, and only the queen is tending it, so it's far easier to handle than a full colony in August. Large nests, ground nests, and anyone in the house who's allergic to stings are a job for a pest control professional.

In winter, the yard looks empty, but not entirely. Somewhere under those leaves or behind that bark, next year's wasps are sitting out the cold. Unless one is tucked in beside the back door, it can stay right where it is.

Recent findings suggest that hydrangeas really have their moment during the summer months, and then spend the winter looking dead, brown, and crispy while we politely look away. Shea McGee, however, has made a point of doing the opposite, and to beautiful effect!

Sources indicate that that's right, folks; not only did the Netflix Dream Home Makeover star give her hydrangeas some attention in winter, but she also added them to the star of the show during the holidays: her Christmas tree! And, much like Sarah Jessica Parker's floral Christmas tree, it's one of those oh-so-simple but oh-so-effective ideas that we can't believe we didn't think of first.

It has been revealed that as you may or may not know, Shea grows Limelight hydrangeas at her Salt Lake City home, telling fans that the blooms “bring me so much joy in the summer”. Is it any wonder, then, that when the interior designer shared a video of her Christmas decor to Instagram, the blooms were front and center?

Industry observers note that A post shared by McGee & Co. (@mcgeeandco).

As you can see above, Shea McGee has decorated her tree with warm brown, tan, and cream ornaments, dried orange slices, clip-on LED candlesticks, and dried hydrangeas from her own garden (although you can buy ready-to-go cone hydrangeas from McGee & Co if you prefer an easier life).

Industry observers note that it's a beyond brilliant idea, as it means the blooms get a second act, which is a better return than most shrubs give you. If you want a similar look, just read on for some tips from the experts.

Shop Shea McGee-Inspired Christmas Decor:.

Keen to give it a whirl from scratch? Look this way...

According to recent reports, cameron of DreamHowYouLive favors Limelight (the same as Shea McGee grows) and Annabelle for a hydrangea arrangement. “Their petals dry stiff and papery, so they keep their shape, where softer mopheads crumble.”.

Flower farmer-florist Joey McFarland of Flowers by Dr. Jo agrees that panicle types like Limelight are best for long stems. He warns that bigleaf hydrangeas set buds in fall, so cutting too deeply means “cutting off your blooms for next year.” Shopping for plants? Browse our list of panicle hydrangea varieties.

Timing is highly important as well, especially when it comes to hydrangeas. Morgan Brooks of Plant Style Home waits until the heads “turn papery and antique in early fall.” Cut too soon and, as Cameron warns, “they wilt instead of drying.” (Which means you need to show patience, grasshopper).

In a recent development, when it comes to drying hydrangeas the experts all have a different opinion, which tells you how difficult it can actually be. Floral preservation artist Nadi Melam of Florals Memories claims, “I always dry hydrangeas in a vase of water,” about an inch, for a “lovely muted antique color.”.

Cameron hangs them upside down in a dark, dry spot for two or three weeks, since vase-dried heads “tend to droop.” Our guide to drying hydrangea flowers covers both.

The best rule to follow if you want the Shea McGee effect? Water-drying holds shape and color well, while air-drying is quicker but leaves blooms more fragile.

Recent findings suggest that there’s one place where most people go wrong when drying hydrangeas for Shea McGee-style decor. As Cameron tells me me he cuts the head town to 3-inch stems, wires each branch and tucks the whole bloom into a gap. His personal rule: “Three small clusters spread around the tree look intentional. One substantial bunch at the top looks like a mistake.”.

In a recent development, arslan Ali of DecoroDea advises, “Treat them like picks, not ornaments,” and says to place them last, “after the ornaments and lights are already on,” so you fill the gaps that are actually still dark. Brooks wires clusters low near the trunk first, then moves smaller heads toward the tips. In essence, you can take a bit from every expert tip.

According to recent reports, for McGee’s look, add dried orange slices, cream and tan ornaments, and warm white lights. Bright white, Cameron notes, makes “the whole thing look cold.”.

Dried petals shed, which is why Melam is so blunt with their advice: “You lose petals every time you touch a flower.” Cameron’s fix is a light hairspray mist that “keeps the shedding down.” And, as for those annoying relatives, who “just want to adjust one thing,” tell them that your Shea McGee-inspired Christmas tree is now a museum exhibit, so hands off".

It has been revealed that if you don't have real hydrangeas in your yard, faux hydrangeas as a no-mess alternative. These cream-white stems give the same soft look without the shedding.

Hydrangeas are also toxic if chewed, so keep clusters out of reach of curious pets.

Sources indicate that those candles on Shea McGee’s Christmas tree? Make them LED.

Melam claims, “Open flame is a no-no since the dry material will ignite right away.” As for saving them for next year, the experts are once again split.

According to recent reports, want a warm glow like MsGee's but without the fire risk? These warm white, dimmable clip-on LED candles come with a remote, so you can keep real flames far from your dried hydrangeas.

Melam stores heads flat in a box with tissue between layers, and Cameron has reused the same heads two years running. However, McFarland states dried blooms “won’t do particularly well in storage” and suggests composting them and cutting fresh ones.

Either way, it’s a good excuse to plant more hydrangeas and see what tip works best for you.

Recent findings suggest that the increasingly common term “eco-friendly” encourages us to think more carefully about the products and practices we use every day. When applied to hardscaping, it brings to mind materials and techniques that minimize environmental impacts and reduce our carbon footprints.

It’s exciting to have such a vast and diverse selection of landscape materials available for our designs and garden improvements, but many of those options have a significant impact on our planet through their creation, shipping, and installation. By thinking about how our hardscaping choices affect natural resources, pollution, and local ecosystems, we can create landscapes that are attractive, functional, and potentially more affordable.

Sources indicate that with 30 years of experience as a landscape designer, I’ve recommended countless decks, patios, paths, fences, and other hardscaping elements to my clients, admittedly with minimal guidance about the actual materials used. In recent years, I’ve seen a notable uptick in clients who have expressed strong interest in locally sourced materials and in repurposing or recycling materials for these features.

Some have even accumulated reclaimed bricks, large concrete pieces, and other materials with the intent of incorporating them into the design. This is exciting to me, as designs should balance the durability and longevity of products with a focus on resource efficiency and environmentally friendly options. These creative approaches are becoming more readily available and are being sought out by eco-savvy gardeners.

Read More: How Space and Structure Create a Living Oasis.

Conventional hardscape materials have a “production history” that often comes with a heavy environmental cost. This might include the lumber we purchase, edging materials, or the pavers and path materials we specify. Their history includes not only energy and resources used in production but also shipping and transport, and ultimately, their disposal or reuse at the end of their useful lives.

According to recent reports, finding lower-impact materials takes some research, but sustainability doesn’t have to come at the expense of durability or functionality. Interestingly, eco-friendly options can be more cost-effective over the long run because of lower maintenance needs and durability.

Recent findings suggest that hardscaping elements such as decks and fences are great examples to explore. Decades ago, the question for clients in my Midwest location was “cedar or treated pine” for most fences or decks. Now, the evolution and wider availability of composite decking and recycled plastic lumber have created increasingly popular alternatives.

According to recent reports, of course, the manufacture of composite lumber isn’t carbon neutral, and its environmental benefits depend on the materials and manufacturing processes involved. However, products incorporating recycled materials can reduce demand for virgin resources, and their durability may offer advantages over time.

Another option for traditional wood features is to seek out responsibly sourced, third-party-certified lumber, such as wood carrying Forest Stewardship Council (FSC) certification. This certification means the wood and products were harvested, processed, and tracked according to established environmental and sourcing standards.

Industry observers note that patios are another popular garden feature, and while I appreciate a nicely installed patio made with concrete, fresh pavers, or bricks, there are some other options available. It is key to consider the permeability of our pavement selections as challenges of runoff and erosion come into play.

Permeable pavers, open-grid pavers, and some types of pervious concrete can allow water to pass through the surface and into underlying layers, helping reduce runoff when properly installed and maintained.

Recent findings suggest that repurposing brick or other paving materials from another project is also an opportunity to add a vintage look and possibly save money. I have a client who obtained more than 4,000 free vitrified clay pavers from the early 1900s (used for streets!) that we used for his paths and patios, and they look fabulous. Reusing these durable materials also kept them in circulation rather than requiring newly manufactured pavers.

Don’t neglect to check out the wide range of energy-efficient lighting options for your landscape as well.

Sources indicate that I’ve also been involved with some rustic patios made of upcycled concrete pieces that were fitted together like puzzle pieces, the gaps filled with plants. Research “urbanite” patios and paths, and see the amazing results!

It’s a great use of a common material that frequently ends up in our landfills. Crushed concrete is another useful material for paths. It can also be used as a base layer for paths and patios, provided it is suitable for the intended application. Again, local sourcing can reduce the carbon footprint associated with shipping and transportation.

Our reasons for supporting eco-friendly hardscaping decisions in our landscapes include, of course, preventing waste, conserving resources, and protecting our local and regional ecosystems and habitats.

While the convenience of buying readily available latest materials may be appealing, taking the time to look into salvaged, recycled, locally sourced, and responsibly manufactured alternatives can yield equally attractive results.

In a recent development, whether you’re planning a new patio, replacing an aging deck, or adding a garden path, find out what materials might already be available for reuse. Explore these opportunities!

#102176. Latest Update: What Your Snake Plant Needs in November – 5 Winter Care Checks to Keep It Glossy and Thriving

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1155 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Gardeningknowhow ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: What Your Snake Plant Needs in November – 5 Winter Care Checks to Keep It Glossy and Thriving

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1155 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Most of the year, a snake plant really is about as hard to kill as people say.
  • Industry observers note that good snake plant care in winter is mostly about doing less and getting the timing right.
  • Sources indicate that take a few minutes with your plant in front of you and work through five checks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most of the year, a snake plant really is about as hard to kill as people say. But that changes in November. The days get short, and the heat comes on, and the watering habit you kept all summer now leaves the potting mix wet for weeks. Yellow leaves and soft, mushy bases tend to follow.

Industry observers note that good snake plant care in winter is mostly about doing less and getting the timing right. Once light levels drop, your snake plant isn't growing much, so it uses far less water and needs no fertilizer at all. What it does need is a dry pot between drinks, steady room temperatures, and a spot out of the cold air that pools along windows.

Sources indicate that take a few minutes with your plant in front of you and work through five checks. Run through them now, then again on a gray afternoon in December. That alone considerably cuts the odds of losing a snake plant to winter.

Sources indicate that don't rely on a calendar when watering snake plants. A snake plant that needed water every two weeks in July might go a month or more between drinks in November. Its surface won't tell you much. So how do you know when it's dry? Push a finger down as far as it goes, or try the chopstick trick: push a wooden skewer to the bottom of the pot and pull it out. Damp mix clings to the wood and darkens it; dry mix leaves it clean.

If you're struggling to know when to water, then use a moisture meter for an accurate assessment, like the Xlux instant read probe, available from Amazon. Water only when the whole depth comes up dry, then let the pot drain fully. Leaves that go soft or flop over at the soil line usually mean the roots have sat wet too long.

Low light is something a snake plant tolerates, not something it grows well in. In November, the sun sits lower and the days are short, so a dim corner that was fine in June may now get very little light. Growth slows, and the mix stays wet far longer because the plant is barely drawing water.

It has been revealed that A spot within a few feet (about a meter) of an east or west window helps. Make the move gradual, though – a plant that goes straight from a dim hallway into hours of direct south sun can scorch.

Without a bright window, a grow light like the Sansi Pot-Clip-On Grow Light, positioned a foot or so (30 cm) above the leaves, fills the gap.

Sources indicate that on a cold evening, hold the back of your hand near the window where your snake plant sits. Chilly on your skin means chilly on the leaves, too. Blame single-pane glass, the gap under an outside door, or a nearby heating vent. Any of them can swing the temperature more than a snake plant can take – even while the thermostat reads fine.

According to recent reports, ordinary room temperatures are what you're after, roughly 60–85°F (16–29°C). Trouble starts if the plant sits below about 50°F (10°C) for long stretches. Leaves pressed against cold glass can develop soft, water-soaked patches. So at night, pull the pot back a foot or two (30–60cm) from the window.

If you want to see what the plant goes through after dark, then use a high/low thermometer, like the TempPro digital indoor thermometer, which displays both high and low temperature and humidity levels.

According to recent reports, tip the pot and look underneath. Drainage holes get plugged with compacted mix, a stray pebble, or roots that have grown through. In a decorative cachepot, a snake plant can stand in an inch (2.5 cm) of old water without anyone noticing. Lift it out and check. If the mix is still wet a week or more after you watered, it may have broken down and is holding too much moisture.

It has been revealed that winter is a poor time to disturb roots, so repotting snake plants is normally a spring job. The exception is a pot that won't drain at all – or a mix that stays soggy no matter what. Then a careful repot now beats rotting roots in March. For a replacement, choose a pot with a drainage hole and its own saucer, like this Vigoro ceramic planter from Home Depot. Fill it with a gritty potting mix, like Miracle-Gro Cactus, Palm, and Citrus Mix, which drains much faster than regular potting soil.

Look each leaf over, down to the soil line, for signs of common snake plant problems. If yellow is creeping up from the base and the leaf feels soft or mushy there, you're looking at overwatering and rotting roots. Cold damage can look a lot like it, though. Wrinkled or curling leaves usually mean the reverse: the plant went too long between drinks.

Sources indicate that next, check the crevices where leaves overlap for pests. Cottony white tufts there are mealybugs (Planococcus citri), and small tan or brown bumps that stay put when nudged are scale (Coccus hesperidum).

Dab a few with a cotton swab dipped in rubbing alcohol, then follow up with a ready-to-use insecticidal soap, like Garden Safe insecticidal soap, sprayed right onto the insects. It's far easier to deal with a dozen now than hundreds in February.

Put the fertilizer away until spring. A plant that isn't actively growing can't use the feed, so unused salts build up in the mix and can burn roots. Hold off on routine repotting for the same reason. Fresh mix and a bigger pot push a plant toward new growth right when the light to support it is lowest. Disturbed roots also recover slowly in a cool room.

It has been revealed that don't water your snake plant on a schedule just because the heat is drying out the air. Dry air and dry soil aren't the same thing, and a snake plant copes with dry air far better than it does with wet roots. For the next few months, you want it holding steady, not growing.

Run the same five checks again around the fresh year. In winter, a snake plant mostly needs the right spot and to be left alone. Give it that, and the one looking a bit tired in November is usually putting up new leaves by late spring.

With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success demonstrates that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

#102175. 7 Thanksgiving Scraps to Save for Backyard Birds – Give Them a Helping Hand This Holiday

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1200 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Gardeningknowhow ↗ Open Full Page

7 Thanksgiving Scraps to Save for Backyard Birds – Give Them a Helping Hand This Holiday

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1200 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The holidays often leave us with more food than we know what to do with, don't they?
  • Yes, some everyday ingredients from the feasting table can make welcome treats for backyard birds, offering a little extra nourishment as temperatures drop and the nights draw in (and transform your outdoor space into a welcoming bird sanctuary in the process).
  • Whether you're hoping to see your birth month bird out there, or just happy to offer your kitchen scraps up to any local critters who might make use of them, here's how to use your Thanksgiving leftovers to keep bird feeders filled over the holidays...
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The holidays often leave us with more food than we know what to do with, don't they? Before throwing everything into the compost or bin, though, take a look at your Thanksgiving leftovers; your feathered friends could be very thankful for them!

Yes, some everyday ingredients from the feasting table can make welcome treats for backyard birds, offering a little extra nourishment as temperatures drop and the nights draw in (and transform your outdoor space into a welcoming bird sanctuary in the process).

Whether you're hoping to see your birth month bird out there, or just happy to offer your kitchen scraps up to any local critters who might make use of them, here's how to use your Thanksgiving leftovers to keep bird feeders filled over the holidays...

Before we dive on in, a word of caution: not every Thanksgiving dish is suitable for wildlife, especially as salt, butter, rich sauces and seasonings can make seemingly harmless scraps unsuitable for birds.

The trick? Try to save a few simple ingredients before they make their way into the casserole dish or onto the dinner table. With that caveat in place, then, here are seven Thanksgiving kitchen scraps worth keeping...

Have a few apples left over from your Thanksgiving preparations? Birds such as robins and other fruit-eating visitors will definitely appreciate small pieces of fresh apple.

Cut the flesh into bite-sized chunks, removing the core and seeds first. Bruised apples are fine so long as they're fresh (they're not as fussy as we are!), but discard any mouldy or spoiled pieces. And avoid offering apple pie filling or cooked apples covered in sugar and spices.

Cranberries are a Thanksgiving staple, and you'd better believe that their fresh (and unseasoned, obviously) counterparts make a lovely treat for birds. Offer a few whole or chopped cranberries on a clean feeding tray like this one from MIXXIDEA.

Frozen cranberries are fine, too, once thawed. Just avoid cranberry sauce, as it typically contains added sugar and may include other ingredients birds don't need. Honestly, a little fresh fruit is all that's required.

In a recent development, pecans (again, plain and unsalted) are another holiday favorite that can be shared with feathered visitors, along with walnuts and peanuts. All of these scrummy nuts are rife at Thanksgiving, and all provide fats and protein that can help birds maintain their energy during colder weather.

It has been revealed that take care to chop larger nuts into manageable pieces and check that they haven't been coated in salt, sugar, chocolate or seasoning. Just like the fruit, nuts should be fresh, too, rather than stale or musty.

Corn often features on the Thanksgiving menu in a big way, and a few plain kernels can be offered to garden birds; just set aside a small portion before adding butter, salt or other seasonings.

Sources indicate that cooked or fresh corn kernels can be placed on a feeding tray, but avoid creamed corn, buttery corn casserole and heavily seasoned dishes. Only offer a little at a time, as damp corn can spoil quickly.

If pumpkin or squash features in your holiday cooking (or your Thanksgiving decor, if you're Kristin Davis!), don't throw away all those seeds; instead, rinse away any stringy pulp, remove any seasoning and allow the seeds to dry thoroughly.

Offer them (have I gotten too repetitive yet?) plain and unsalted, either whole for larger birds or broken into smaller pieces for smaller visitors. They're a useful source of fats and nutrients, making them a worthwhile addition to your bird feeding station.

According to recent reports, leftover rice can also be shared with birds from your Thanksgiving feast, provided it hasn't been cooked with salt, butter, oil, garlic or onions. Both white and brown rice are suitable in small quantities when prepared plainly.

According to recent reports, P.S. There's a persistent myth that uncooked or cooked rice swells inside birds and causes harm, but this isn't true. Nevertheless, rice shouldn't replace more nutritious bird food, so just offer just a small amount (you may find your birth month winter bird adores it) and remove anything uneaten so it doesn't have a chance to go bad.

It has been revealed that A little leftover boiled or baked potato from your Thanksgiving prep can be another treat for your feathered friends. Set aside a portion before adding butter, milk, salt or gravy, then allow it to cool and chop it into small pieces.

Please never offer raw potatoes or green potato peelings, and avoid chips, roast potatoes cooked in fat and heavily seasoned mashed potatoes. Experts always advise that plain potato be treated as an occasional extra rather than a regular food source.

It's every bit as important to know what to avoid when it comes to feeding birds your Thanksgiving leftovers. Turkey fat and pan drippings might seem like an easy substitute for bird suet, but they're best kept off the feeding station. Audubon, in fact, warns that turkey fat melts more readily than traditional suet and can turn rancid quickly. It can also smear onto feathers, potentially affecting their waterproofing and insulation.

Sources indicate that gravy, stuffing and salty side dishes should also stay off the menu, as they often contain butter, salt, onion and garlic, none of which are suitable additions to a wild bird's diet. Avoid, too, anything that contains chocolate, along with avocado, sugary desserts and heavily processed foods, too. Bread and pastry aren't particularly nutritious (even if they won't do any harm), so think up some better ways to use your leftovers; might this author humbly submit the idea of a bread-and-butter pudding?

Once you've picked all of the bird-friendly scraps out of your Thanksgiving feast, be sure to present it properly! Always use a clean feeding tray rather than leaving piles of food on the ground, and try to put food out in the morning, as this is when it's most likely to be eaten.

According to recent reports, take care to remove anything uneaten before it spoils, and wash feeding surfaces regularly to reduce the risk of bacteria and disease spreading. It's also worth keeping fresh drinking water available, particularly as colder weather approaches, and remember that kitchen scraps are supposed to be occasional extras, not a replacement for a balanced wild bird food mix.

Still, all those warnings aside, there's no denying that sharing a little of your holiday feast with your local birds is a lovely way to give thanks to Mother Nature (and reduce food waste at the same time).

GPOD on the Road: Shakespeare Garden in Evanston, Illinois

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (712 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Finegardening

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Perhaps he was hiding somewhere in the shade on that hot June day!
  • According to recent reports, earlier this week, I shared a look at the historic sunken garden connecting two homes built for sisters in Wilmette, Illinois.
  • According to recent reports, tucked away on Northwestern University’s campus, the Shakespeare Garden has been around for more than a century!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“O Romeo, Romeo, wherefore art thou Romeo?”.

Perhaps he was hiding somewhere in the shade on that hot June day!

According to recent reports, earlier this week, I shared a look at the historic sunken garden connecting two homes built for sisters in Wilmette, Illinois. Today, we’re taking a look at another beautiful garden and a little Shakespearean history.

According to recent reports, tucked away on Northwestern University’s campus, the Shakespeare Garden has been around for more than a century! It all started in 1915, when the Garden Club of Evanston decided to create a garden to commemorate the 300th anniversary of Shakespeare’s death and celebrate the ties between England and America during World War I. They brought in renowned Danish-American landscape architect Jens Jensen to design the space, and by 1920, the club had completed planting a collection inspired by more than 50 plants mentioned in Shakespeare’s works. How neat! The garden was officially dedicated in 1930 and added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1988.

Industry observers note that the Garden Club of Evanston still cares for the garden today, and it’s a wonderful little place to visit. Enjoy!

While wandering the shady paths at the back of the garden, I came across this natural doorway formed by the trees. What a beautiful view of the central lawn and sundial! Jensen wanted the formal garden to feel like a clearing in the woods, and I think he achieved just that.

The garden measures just 70 by 100 feet and is made up of eight planting beds originally arranged in a formal knot-garden design. (If you’re not familiar with knot gardens, look them up! They’re amazing!) In 1990, English garden designer John Brookes recommended removing some of the boxwood (Buxus cvs., Zones 4–9) to make room for more perennials and a more relaxed planting style. He also had the sundial moved to the center to create a stronger focal point.

According to recent reports, the garden underwent a renovation in 2016 to restore several of its historic features, including the wooden obelisks seen here, stone benches, and pathways. The project also included replacing declining plants to help preserve the original design.

My favorite view of the garden! Formally informal.

Jensen’s original planting list included everything from columbines (Aquilegia vulgaris, Zones 3–8) and violets (Viola spp., Zones 3–9) to poppies (Papaver somniferum, annual), peonies (Paeonia officinalis, Zones 4–8), and lavender (Lavandula angustifolia, Zones 5–8), all plants mentioned in Shakespeare’s writings. The plantings have changed over the years, but the garden still celebrates that connection.

According to recent reports, last, but certainly not least, this Elizabethan-style stone bench was installed in 1929, along with the garden’s memorial fountain. Nearly a century later, it’s still a beautiful spot to sit and enjoy the surroundings!

The Shakespeare Garden is open to the public, and I highly recommend stopping by if you’re ever in the area! You can learn more about its history and plan your visit through the Garden Club of Evanston’s website.

Latest Update: How to Design a Garden That Solves Problems and Invites You In

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1058 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Finegardening

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • People often ask how I approach the garden design process and what information I gather before developing a initiative.
  • I like to create purpose-driven designs.
  • Design is all about solving problems and connecting clients to their gardens, usually beginning with a questionnaire to bring all those unspoken needs to light.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

People often ask how I approach the garden design process and what information I gather before developing a initiative. While every client and garden is different, I usually start with the same basic questions.

I like to create purpose-driven designs. For example, I’m often called on to solve a problem, even if it is simply “I have a newly introduced house and a blank slate.” It may be just a section of the garden, the front yard, or something specific like repairing a garden after a new septic system installation or after a new house is built next door.

Design is all about solving problems and connecting clients to their gardens, usually beginning with a questionnaire to bring all those unspoken needs to light. Questions help people consider things they would not normally think about. As a result, these conversations define their needs and desires, helping me combine different elements into a cohesive design.

Recent findings suggest that the same approach applies to projects in my own garden. I don’t give myself a questionnaire, but I do ask myself the same questions. First, I assess the challenges, the location of the area in relation to the rest of the property, and the environmental conditions that will influence the planting.

In a new garden, the major goal is often screening. Most people want privacy to live their lives outside without having to see a neighboring house, road, commercial area, or vacant lot.

It has been revealed that privacy was one of the big considerations when planning my grass garden. There was no privacy between my property and the neighboring property. I could see my neighbors eat their dinner, watch them play with their grandchildren, and even see them argue. Their house was also too close to the property line, and in fact, their sidewalk was on my property. That was a problem.

Because the sidewalk was already there when I moved in, I had to incorporate it into my design, but I could still make it disappear visually.

I started out with some tall elements at the back of the bed to start the screening process. I positioned these plants so I could maintain them from my property without having branches extend over the property line. Keeping their mature size in mind also helped avoid potential conflicts with the neighboring property. Soft screens made of trees and tall shrubs (both evergreen and deciduous) offer privacy without creating a harsh, artificial boundary line.

Read More: 20 Unique Hedging Plant Options.

In a recent development, looking at the space, I could see a definite focal point within my property. With the neighbor behind me, the view naturally led the eye toward the water. Therefore, I designed a one-sided border rather than an island bed meant to be viewed from multiple directions. Making the border as deep as 20 feet in places gave me enough room to continue screening the neighboring property while also providing some sound buffering.

In a recent development, understanding the environmental conditions was the next step. The back edge is on the north side of my property. The large trees and shrubs would not shade the rest of the bed. This meant the bed would be in full sun all day, all season long.

What a challenge for this PNW native who grew up mostly in the forest (or woods, as we called it). I had to learn about plants that liked full sun, drying winds, and dry soil so they could thrive. Rather than trying to re-create the shaded woodland conditions I knew best, I needed to work with what the site naturally offered.

Read More: Summer-Dry Gardening: A Visit to Beth Chatto’s Gravel Garden.

Sources indicate that growing up in the forest, I longed for wide-open sky and long views. Above all, I wanted to immerse myself in the garden. A long row of hedging plants that I could only look at wasn’t what I had in mind. I wanted to become part of the blowing, rustling movement of the grasses. While experiencing the plants, I also wanted to connect with insects, pollinators, birds, frogs, and even a few rabbits.

Recent findings suggest that I consider the challenge met. The amount of wildlife activity surrounding me in the garden never ceases to amaze me. I feel as if I’m in a different world while surrounded by all the action and movement of the grasses and perennials, far away from massive cedar trees, moss, and ferns. Sun, wind, fragrant flowers, and the smell of warm earth are all-encompassing there.

Industry observers note that even during the winter, this garden pulls me out, bundled up and coffee in hand, to see what is happening. Early spring bulbs push through the soil, mice shelter under the evergreen sedges, and birds search for a breakfast of grass seeds and gather bits and pieces to build newly introduced nests.

The ultimate goal of any designer is finding the right outdoor elements to pull people outside and connect them with nature. Those elements are individual to each client. They could be an eating area, outdoor kitchen, hot tub, play area, pond, fountain, or hidden sitting area. Maybe the goal is plant-driven, with a vegetable garden, cutting garden, or collection of conifers.

When these features are thoughtfully integrated with immersive, naturalistic plantings, the result is an outdoor space that invites people to experience their gardens throughout the year.

Discuss this article or ask gardening questions with a regional gardening expert on the Gardening Answers forum.

And for more Pacific Northwest regional reports, click here.

Susan Calhoun is the owner and principal designer of Plantswoman Design in Bainbridge Island, Washington.

It’s a great mix of foliage colors and textures even when everything isn’t in bloom.

Industry observers note that I love the placement of the patio and pathway. It’s a really useful design technique for maximizing every square inch of a small garden while still leaving plenty of room for outdoor living.

Recent findings suggest that absolutely gorgeous section of the garden! This is where we really start to feel like we’re in the tropics. ‘Mars Madness’ hardy hibiscus (Hibiscus ‘Mars Madness’, Zones 4–9) has all the tropical drama while still being hardy enough for a Minneapolis winter. And it’s hard to miss those giant cannas and the colorful foliage on the coleus. I love all the red blooms too!

In a recent development, one of Arianne’s fabulous container combinations features Tropicanna Gold canna (Canna ‘Mactro’, Zones 8–11), purple shield (Strobilanthes dyerianus, annual), begonias (Begonia cvs., annual), flowering kale (Brassica oleracea, annual), and parrot’s beak (Lotus berthelotii, annual). So much of the color and interest here comes from foliage!

There is so much to look at in this section of the garden! Those variegated geranium leaves are striking, and I could go on and on about Arianne’s use of color and texture. The apple tree surrounded by all these ornamentals is an unexpected but lovely touch.

Recent findings suggest that just around the corner from the photo above. Another gorgeous tropical container, and ‘Blue Shadow’ fothergilla (Fothergilla × intermedia ‘Blue Shadow’, Zones 5–8) grows on the left in this view.

Sources indicate that another view of the backyard borders. There are so many plants packed into this garden, you would never believe this is a small urban backyard. And, if my eyes are working correctly, I’d say that’s a clover lawn?!

Tall conifers create a fantastic privacy screen in this view. The garden really is its own secluded paradise.

A shady combination of hostas, ‘Banana Boat’ sedge (Carex siderosticha ‘Banana Boat’, Zones 4–9), painted fern, purple shield, coleus, and impatiens.

Zinnias, statice, amaranth, and overwintered dahlias are just some of the blooms that make their way into bouquets for friends, family, and coworkers. So pretty!

Thank you so much for sharing your garden with us again, Arianne! It’s always a treat to see what you and Micah are growing, and I think I could spend hours wandering around this garden and still find something new to admire.

#102171. Details for Durable Decks

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1300 w)
