Details for Durable Decks

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1300 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Finehomebuilding

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that in this article, tech editor Mark Petersen discusses some aspects of deck building that may not be addressed by the building code or caught during a deck permit plan review or site inspection.
  • I’ve built a lot of decks, some still standing after 30-plus years.
  • On the flip side, I’ve come across structures that range from somewhat wobbly to absolutely unsafe due to feeble footings, poorly installed or absent ledger flashing, undersized framing, and missing or misused hardware and fasteners.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that in this article, tech editor Mark Petersen discusses some aspects of deck building that may not be addressed by the building code or caught during a deck permit plan review or site inspection. He focuses on building secure footings, ensuring proper ledger fastening, avoiding flashing mistakes, using correct connectors, and strengthening the framing.

I’ve built a lot of decks, some still standing after 30-plus years. I’ve also worked with several deck-building rock stars to create articles on the subject. I’ve even helped companies like Trex create a bunch of how-to content. In all my years of research and hands-on experience, I’ve seen plenty of examples of decks built to last.

On the flip side, I’ve come across structures that range from somewhat wobbly to absolutely unsafe due to feeble footings, poorly installed or absent ledger flashing, undersized framing, and missing or misused hardware and fasteners.

Building to code and following the requirements spelled out by your local building department will get you most of the way to a safe and durable deck, but even a code-compliant deck can be improved with some due diligence and attention to detail.

In this article, I’ve focused on some vulnerabilities that may not be addressed by the building code or caught during a deck permit strategy review or site inspection. Think of this as an above-and-beyond checklist of details worth considering on your next deck build..

Drawing by Christopher Mills. Click here to enlarge.

According to recent reports, for years I worked for a production builder. They used to insulate a home’s rim-joist cavity with batt insulation and no vapor retarder, which was code-approved at the time. This caused all sorts of moisture damage from water vapor that was driven through the cavity.

Industry observers note that instead of switching to rigid or spray foam, their first fix was to install SIP rim joists, the most common of which have a core of EPS insulation sandwiched between OSB sheathing. This solution lasted less than a year because uninformed deck builders and homeowners assumed they could use standard lag screws to then attach deck ledgers to the rim joist.

The result was that most of those fasteners were secured to only the two layers of plywood that made up the SIP, rather than solid-sawn lumber—a serious problem when the connection is responsible for supporting the deck.

In a recent development, so, don’t assume there’s a conventional solid-sawn rim joist behind the sheathing. The floor system might include an SIP rim joist or floor trusses with just a ribbon board instead of a solid ledger. When building a new deck, a permit plan review or site inspection will hopefully catch this, but if you are resurfacing an existing deck, now is the time to confirm a solid ledger connection.

It has been revealed that if you discover an SIP rim joist or a floor system that can’t support a conventional ledger connection, try to track down the manufacturer of the components in question for an approved attachment solution. If that’s not an option, you could consult an engineer or add a beam and posts near the house and build the deck as a freestanding structure.

Don’t attach a deck ledger to the rim joist of a cantilevered bump-out or bay window, or directly to a stud wall.

Recent findings suggest that neither provides the load path assumed by conventional prescriptive ledger details. Nevertheless, this was common practice back in the day.

In fact, the ledger on my own son’s house is attached to a bay. A site inspection will likely catch this code violation, but if you are just making cosmetic improvements that don’t require a permit, do your due diligence.

In some cases, these connections can be made to work, but they typically require an engineered design and structural modifications, which might involve tearing into a finished ceiling to add blocking or other framing reinforcement. As with any questionable ledger connection, the simpler solution is to treat the deck as freestanding.

In a recent development, add a beam and posts close to the house so the deck loads are carried directly to footings rather than relying on a questionable ledger connection. That’s the fix I proposal to make on my son’s house. In the meantime, I warned him against throwing any parties on the deck.

In my work as a contractor, I replaced several patio doors after either the door sill or ledger flashing failed, allowing water to rot the subfloor and some of the framing below it. I came across this problem primarily when deck boards were installed right up under the door sill, where splashing rain and melting Minnesota snow combined to wreak havoc over the years. To help prevent this, whenever possible I would install the deck a few inches below the door sill. I also instructed my customers to keep snow from piling up against the door.

The main hurdle to installing a deck below the door sill is maintaining proper ledger-fastener placement. On a large deck, the ledger may be as deep as the house rim joist and dropping it a few inches can make it impossible to meet the required fastener edge distances in both the ledger and the rim joist. One solution is to use smaller deck joists and reduce their span by adding another beam. If this doesn’t work, you may need to consult an engineer for an alternative connection detail.

Of course, lowering the deck surface below the door sill isn’t as much of a concern in warm, dry regions—and it isn’t always an option when someone in the house has mobility challenges.

Drawing by Christopher Mills. Click here to enlarge.

In a recent development, the only deck callback I ever received happened after the first time I worked with composite fascia boards. I didn’t use enough fasteners. I thought the manufacturer’s recommended screw spacing was preposterous overkill, but I was wrong. The fascia buckled, and I returned to the scene, tail between my legs, to add more screws.

In addition to protecting your reputation, following manufacturer recommendations can also preserve warranties. If you use unapproved fasteners or hidden clips on composite decking and there’s a factory defect, some companies might not stand behind their product. Most factory warranties stipulate using only approved installation methods and materials.

Double-check that the structural hardware you grab is rated for exterior use with the treated lumber you’re using. I nearly walked out of a home center with interior-grade joist hangers that were in the wrong bin. They looked almost identical to the exterior versions. Also, don’t mix stainless-steel and galvanized connectors and fasteners; dissimilar metals can accelerate corrosion.

Sources indicate that just as important, use the fasteners specified by the connector manufacturer. Short hanger nails, roofing nails, deck screws, and whatever happens to be in your tool pouch aren’t necessarily acceptable substitutes. Pay particular attention to double-shear hangers: The angled fasteners often need to be longer than the face nails so they penetrate through the joist and well into the supporting member. And fill the required holes—structural hardware only provides its rated capacity when it’s installed the way it was tested.

For comprehensive info on deck hardware, including fastener and hardware options and how each connection works to keep the deck structure intact, check out Mike Guertin’s video series, “Critical Deck-Framing Connections.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that hi GPOD! Today we’re heading to Hingham, Massachusetts, for some beautiful fall color from Nancy. Nancy sent in photos of the trees and shrubs winding down the season in her garden, along with one of the last flowers still hanging on.

This is our sugar maple (Acer saccharum, Zones 3–8) showing off its fall foliage before it drops its leaves to keep my gardens warm this winter.

My ‘Forest Pansy’ eastern redbud (Cercis canadensis ‘Forest Pansy’, Zones 5–9) is maroon most of the year until fall, when it turns a lovely yellow.

My paperbark maple (Acer griseum, Zones 4–8) has had a hard time coping with our summer droughts and water restrictions, but it looked a lovely red this fall.

In a recent development, this is another native tree that many people are not familiar with, fringe tree (Chionanthus virginicus, Zones 4–9), which has fragrant white flowers hanging from its branches in late spring to early summer. As you can see, it also looks beautiful in its yellow fall foliage.

It has been revealed that in the front of this picture is a young sweetgum (Liquidambar styraciflua, Zones 5–9), which has spectacular red color in the fall and develops spiky seed balls as it matures. In the distance is a blackhaw viburnum (Viburnum prunifolium, Zones 3–9) showing its orange fall color.

‘Mount Airy’ fothergilla (Fothergilla ‘Mount Airy’, Zones 5–8) glows red and orange in front of fragrant abelia (Abelia mosanensis, Zones 4–8), whose fall color is beginning to fade. The abelia will charm us all again in spring with its fragrant blooms.

According to recent reports, sweetshrub (Calycanthus floridus, Zones 5–9) on the right has turned a lovely yellow. Amazingly, all three sweetshrubs shown here had the bark eaten off around every trunk by rabbits last winter, killing every one. They all grew back from the roots, showing just how resilient they are. On the left, ‘Mount Airy’ fothergilla is showing off its red fall foliage, and in back is ‘Alice’ oakleaf hydrangea (Hydrangea quercifolia ‘Alice’, Zones 5–9) with maroon fall foliage.

One of the only flowers left blooming is ‘Sheffield Pink’ chrysanthemum (Chrysanthemum ‘Sheffield Pink’, Zones 5–9), which complements the dark foliage of Diabolo ninebark (Physocarpus opulifolius ‘Monlo’, Zones 3–7) behind it.

Industry observers note that thanks for sharing your fall garden with us, Nancy! Nancy says she’s ready to wander the garden, make her list of what needs dividing in spring, and figure out what fresh plants need to be bought. Sounds like a good way to spend the off-season to me!

Keep Ducts Where They Belong

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2463 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Finehomebuilding

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, installing HVAC equipment and ductwork in unconditioned attics can increase energy costs, reduce comfort, and contribute to air leakage, condensation, mold growth, and indoor air quality problems.
  • Industry observers note that for decades, houses have been built with forced-air ductwork and heating and cooling equipment in unconditioned attics.
  • It has been revealed that my manufacturer, Aarow Building, has been building high-performance homes in Missouri for going on three decades now.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, installing HVAC equipment and ductwork in unconditioned attics can increase energy costs, reduce comfort, and contribute to air leakage, condensation, mold growth, and indoor air quality problems. Plenum trusses create dedicated spaces above ceilings for ductwork and other mechanical systems within the home’s conditioned envelope, helping maintain consistent ceiling heights while improving energy efficiency and durability. Successful implementation requires early coordination among builders, architects, HVAC designers, and truss manufacturers, along with carefully planned duct layouts and continuous, airtight control layers to prevent moisture problems and ensure long-term performance.

Industry observers note that for decades, houses have been built with forced-air ductwork and heating and cooling equipment in unconditioned attics. The wide-open, easy-to-access attic space makes the practice common, convenient, and familiar for the framing and mechanical trades. But from a building-performance standpoint, it’s a terrible idea. Vented attics are extremely hot in summer and cold in winter, so every foot of duct placed in that location exposes the conditioned air within the ductwork to temperatures way beyond those inside the house.

It has been revealed that my manufacturer, Aarow Building, has been building high-performance homes in Missouri for going on three decades now. We have a hot, humid climate and—like in many places—attic ductwork is common here, so we’ve seen plenty of examples of what can happen when you install HVAC equipment in an unconditioned space.

According to recent reports, for starters, the extreme temperature difference between the conditioned air inside the ducts and the temperature outside them results in a house that uses more energy and is more expensive to heat and cool compared to a house with an HVAC system inside the conditioned space. And the additional expense isn’t limited to operational costs. HVAC ducts and equipment in unconditioned spaces must have higher capacities to compensate for the adverse conditions where they’re located, meaning the systems are more expensive.

Sources indicate that higher costs are not the only downsides. Supply and return air leaks are common with HVAC systems in attics and are problematic from a building-durability and performance perspective. Supply leaks waste conditioned air and pressurize the attic, which depressurizes the house, causing additional air leakage in the conditioned space—and in extreme scenarios, backdrafting of combustion appliances.

In a recent development, backdrafting can release carbon monoxide into the home, creating a serious risk of poisoning. There’s also a lot of water vapor in flue gasses, which can create humidity problems and mold growth. Equally common are return leaks that pull dusty, humid, or hot attic air into the heating or cooling system, negatively affecting energy efficiency, occupant comfort, and indoor air quality.

Air-conditioning supply ducts, which are cold, often become condensing surfaces. Condensing water can ruin finishes and lead to mold growth that may or may not be visible. Mold you can’t see can be especially problematic for sensitive individuals who might experience cold-like symptoms, asthma, or other respiratory problems. Similar problems can occur in cold climates when warm, conditioned air contacts cold spaces, creating condensation and potential mold problems. Even the most reliable HVAC system, when located outside the enclosure, can lead to comfort complaints and callbacks that are hard to diagnose and fix.

Industry observers note that you can avoid all these problems by making room for HVAC ducts inside the house’s conditioned space during the design phase, before the house is built. The concept is not newly introduced—building scientists started advocating for ductwork within conditioned spaces in the late ’80s and early ’90s, and conscientious builders and designers paid attention. They developed methods for hiding ductwork in dropped hallway ceilings and in soffits that run along the tops of walls (see the drawings).

Sources indicate that these methods work—but from a design perspective, employing them can be tough on some homes. I’ve found that soffits in bedrooms are almost always unwanted by designers and clients. I think the best way to hide ducts, both substantial and small, is to place them in ceiling chases using plenum trusses.

In a recent development, my first exposure to plenum trusses came from architect Steve Baczek. For a period, Steve was working with a production builder in the Southwest United States that offered a comfort guarantee for every home they built. One of the ways they ensured comfort was by keeping the HVAC system inside the building envelope. In some parts of the house, Steve hid ductwork in soffits, but he also used plenum trusses in places where soffits were impractical. The idea of using plenum trusses stuck with me.

According to recent reports, we eventually began using plenum trusses in some of our builds for the same reasons as Steve: greater comfort, efficiency, and building durability. In 2017, our company made the decision that ductwork and HVAC equipment would be installed inside the conditioned enclosure whenever possible. In homes with a conditioned attic, the solution is easy. The ducts can simply live in the attic. The same is true when we have a conditioned crawlspace or basement available for distribution.

Many of the homes we build, however, are slab-on-grade with a vented attic above them. Those homes require another strategy, and plenum trusses have become one of our preferred solutions. They allow us to maintain consistent ceiling heights throughout the house while still providing a dedicated space for ductwork and other mechanical systems inside the building envelope. The result gives us the architectural appearance we want without compromising the mechanical strategy, occupant comfort, or energy efficiency.

According to recent reports, plenum trusses are engineered with an open space free of chords and braces that becomes a cavity for ducts, pipes, and refrigeration lines running perpendicular to the trusses. This plenum cavity is lined with an air-impermeable material, typically wood sheathing or drywall for airtightness. Ducts can also be run in angled plenums or in an airtight plenum space made between two trusses, as seen in the photos below.

Parallel Plenum: In this space, eight girder trusses have an opening that allows a duct to pass through them and then turn 90° into a plenum space built on-site from taped sheathing between two of the girder trusses. Both site-built and engineered plenum spaces need a continuous air barrier—in this case, taped sheathing—to prevent air movement through the plenum space.

Recent findings suggest that angled Plenum: To get the conditioned air to its intended registers most efficiently, the main plenum on this project is angled and installed within 10 individually engineered trusses. Each truss has the plenum space offset a few inches from the previous truss’s plenum space, creating the angled plenum. It took about an hour with the truss designer to plan this layout.

Strapped Ceiling: Once the ductwork is installed and sealed and other mechanicals are in place, the ceiling is strapped with 2×4 furring for securing the finished drywall ceiling.

A plenum truss offers a way to design a house’s framing around the mechanical systems, rather than squeezing ductwork into whatever leftover space is available. In simple terms, the bottom chord of a plenum truss is notched with a framed rectangle above, creating a dedicated service cavity, or chase, above the finished ceiling. Importantly, the chase is within the building enclosure, beneath the air, insulation, and vapor control layers—unlike an unconditioned attic, which is essentially outside the building. In addition to ductwork, the plenum space can also house electrical and low-voltage wiring, pipes, and other mechanical systems while keeping them inside the conditioned space of the home.

It has been revealed that the notable point is that the chase is designed, not discovered. You can’t build the chase with field alterations after the trusses arrive. By then, the rooflines, heel heights, load paths, bearing points, ceiling planes, and mechanical layout are already largely locked in. A plenum-truss strategy can only work when the builder, architect, mechanical designer, and truss supplier are involved early on and work together. In my experience, the biggest challenge has been the truss design. Nearly every builder or designer I know who uses plenum trusses has encountered some degree of resistance or hesitation from a truss manufacturer, which I think is understandable. We are asking the truss designer to create something more complicated than a conventional roof truss while accommodating structural loads, duct dimensions, roof geometry, bearing locations, and the other constraints of the building.

The best results we have had come from working directly with the truss designer early in the process. Whenever possible, we sit down with the designer and work through the layout before the trusses are finalized. An extra hour spent with a truss designer is how you end up with a plenum large enough to fit and efficiently route the ducts while framing the complicated rooflines typical of the custom homes we build. Modern truss-design software makes it relatively easy to look at the proposed truss geometry and determine if the plenum will be significant enough and correctly positioned for efficiently routing ducts that are the right size.

Recent findings suggest that plenum ceilings use furred-down framing or drywall-suspension systems to lower the entire ceiling. The system requires a second air barrier above the furred-down section(s), adding significant cost and complexity to the whole ceiling assembly and not just the plenum service cavity.

It has been revealed that lowered ceilings refer to a section of lowered ceiling (often in hallways), and were pioneered by building scientists as a way to keep ductwork in the conditioned space. The system is less expensive than dropping an entire ceiling, but many clients find the lowered portion of ceiling makes the hallway or other space feel oppressive or confining.

Wall-to-ceiling soffits provide a space between the ceiling and the top of built-in cabinetry. Unfortunately, the design is often limited to concealing small ducts, and clients and designers often object to soffits outside the kitchen, especially when they obstruct a view or look like an afterthought.

Industry observers note that conditioned attics bring the insulation, air-control, and vapor-control layers to the roof sheathing, typically with spray foam on the underside of the roof sheathing. But insulating an entire attic with spray foam is expensive, and conditioned attics add a lot of space that must be temperature-controlled, increasing costs over time.

Once the house design is finalized, the next step is to determine where the ducts and equipment need to go. That means the HVAC design must be figured out before the trusses are ordered. The air-handler location, trunk lines, branch runs, register locations, return ducts, and grilles need to be finalized during the design process. A real duct layout matters. A rectangular box on a proposal marked “mechanical” is not enough, so we engage our mechanical design team early in the process and make sure the duct size and routing is specified in their HVAC design. Leaving the duct sizing and routing to whoever highlights up on installation day is never the right approach.

Recent findings suggest that once the duct layout is understood, the truss designer can design the truss framing to accommodate it. The chase needs to be deep and wide enough for the ductwork and anything else other trades require in the plenum space. It also needs to provide reasonable access for the people doing the work. If a duct must be bent, crushed, or forced around a framing member, the truss and/or HVAC design has failed. This is where builders need to be assertive in preconstruction. It’s not enough to simply ask whether the ductwork will fit—the HVAC designers should be able to identify on the plans where it will fit. By the end of the design process, the framing proposal, mechanical plan, and truss drawings must agree with one another.

Sources indicate that A plenum truss only improves building and HVAC performance if the service cavity is within the home’s conditioned enclosure, without any gaps in the control layers. The air-barrier location has to be clear, which can be verified using what building scientist Joe Lstiburek and architect Steve Baczek describe as the “red pen test.” You should be able to trace the home’s entire air barrier location on the plans without lifting a red pen. If the ceiling drywall is the primary air barrier and vapor-control layer, then the plenum needs to be detailed so the ceiling drywall connects to the drywall or sheathing surrounding the plenum cavity, keeping the air- and vapor-control layers continuous. In most cases, this means the plenum is drywalled inside, ducts are installed and sealed, and then ceiling drywall is installed below the plenum, creating a flat ceiling with hidden ductwork above.

We use Zip System sheathing as our air control layer in the plenum space and on the rest of the building enclosure. Our framing crews install and tape the sheathing in the plenum space as part of their framing contract. The material might cost a little more than a drywall air barrier, but we find that having the framers install the air barrier works better with job sequencing than having the drywallers at the project twice, first to install and tape the plenum drywall and a second time to drywall the rest of the house. Whether you use drywall or taped sheathing, the takeaway is the same: All three sides (sides and cap) of the plenum, and where it meets the ceiling drywall, must be airtight.

It has been revealed that the enclosure must also be airtight for vapor control, as most water that condenses on building surfaces and in cavities leading to mold and damage is the result of water vapor carried by air leaks that condenses on cold surfaces. Condensation can occur if the plenum space is not properly sealed from air movement, so you need a continuous air control layer in the plenum space and throughout the rest of the building for effective air and vapor control.

There’s no question that plenum trusses require more preconstruction planning than installing ducts and air handlers in unvented attics, and they typically add to the cost of a truss package. But the upfront planning and additional costs should be weighed against the cost of comfort complaints, wasted energy dollars, mold risk, and the labor involved with sealing penetrations and insulating ducts and HVAC equipment in unvented attics. Keeping ducts and HVAC equipment out of unconditioned spaces makes longer-lasting, more comfortable houses, which makes the additional effort and expense a smart investment for our clients.

In a recent development, — Jake Bruton is the president of Aarow Builders in Columbia, Mo. Photos by the author. Drawings by Dan Thornton.

Sources indicate that I have lived in this house and garden for a little over a year. When I moved here, I worked hard to transplant many of my plants, and the garden continues to be a work in progress.

Delphinium (Delphinium cvs., Zones 3–7) with coleus (Coleus scutellarioides, annual).

Native swamp rose mallow (Hibiscus moscheutos, Zones 5–9) and zinnias.

Perennial begonia (Begonia grandis, Zones 6–9), a soft mahonia bush just planted this spring, and amaranth.

A watermelon my husband grew in our garden area created by a fresh stepped retaining wall.

According to recent reports, A work in progress… I transplanted this hearts-a-bustin’ (Euonymus americanus, Zones 6–9) from a different spot where I originally had it. It was crowded in and now will be able to spread out.

Sources indicate that this celosia (Spicata group) actually grew from seeds of plants that were in a pot last summer. The ground in this area is where a tree used to be, and the roots are rotting and creating wonderful soft soil.

Thanks for sharing another patch from your garden, Connie! And I have to know: What variety of watermelon did your husband grow? It’s huge and oblong! I hope it was delicious. Looking forward to the next update! 🙂.

Fiber-Cement Plank Repair

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (878 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Finehomebuilding

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I need to remove 12 courses of blind-nailed 5-1/4-in.-wide fiber-cement lap siding with a 4-in.
  • It’s challenging to remove blind-nailed fiber-cement lap siding, but patience and an extra set of hands make removing and reinstalling the planks easier.
  • Industry observers note that first, mark out the damaged area with painter’s tape.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I need to remove 12 courses of blind-nailed 5-1/4-in.-wide fiber-cement lap siding with a 4-in. exposure to repair a 5-ft. by 5-ft. section of wall behind it. I’d like to reinstall the old siding without it looking like a repair. What’s the best way to remove fiber-cement lap siding without damaging the planks? How can I make removal and reinstallation less noticeable?

It’s challenging to remove blind-nailed fiber-cement lap siding, but patience and an extra set of hands make removing and reinstalling the planks easier.

Industry observers note that first, mark out the damaged area with painter’s tape. You’ll have to remove full pieces of siding for the repair, so look for the nearest butt joints between individual planks to the left and right of the taped area. Mark the joints in every course of the taped repair area. Plank joints are generally staggered by two studs in successive courses—32 in. or 48 in., depending on the stud spacing. If you’re lucky, the repair area will fit within one 12-ft. plank, so you’ll need to remove just one plank per course between the nearest joints. More likely, you’ll need to remove two. This takes more time, but the removal process is the same.

The first plank is the hardest to remove. Start with the uppermost course in the area you marked out and gently pry up the overlying plank far enough to locate the nails. Then mark the nail locations with small pieces of tape on the overlying course. The butt joints to the left and right of the plank may have been caulked. If so, carefully cut through the sealant with a utility knife.

It has been revealed that when fiber-cement planks are 8 in. or wider, you can lift the bottom edge far enough to pry out the nails from the plank below by slipping a thin flat bar under that plank and up to the shank of the nail. Gently pry the plank up slightly and then remove the flat bar. Press down on the top edge of the plank so the nail head stands proud of the surface, then set the flat bar under the nail head and pry it out.

Sources indicate that prying up narrower planks to pull 2-in. or longer nails often breaks the plank, so in these situations I use a thin cutting tool to cut the nails holding the plank—the Malco Hidden Nail Cutter is made for this job, though you can also use a reciprocating saw with a long metal-cutting blade. Set a 1-ft.-sq. piece of PVC or coil stock under the flat bar to avoid scratching the finish, gently lift the plank up about ¼ in. at each blind nail location, and use the Malco tool or recip saw to cut the nails. Don’t pry too much or you’ll break the top edge of the overlying plank. As you cut the nails, have a helper hold one end of the plank so you can control its removal and be careful sliding the plank downward so the cut-off nails don’t scratch the plank beneath.

With the first plank out of the way, most of the nails holding the next plank down are exposed. Pull the exposed nails using the flat bar method: insert the flat bar between the plank and the wall sheathing at the nail location and pry against the wall; once the nail is broken free and raised 1/4 in., push the top of the plank back against the wall so the nail head is proud, and finish pulling the nail with the flat bar. Cut any blind nails that remain before removing the plank.

Continue working down, removing planks left and right as close to the taped-out area as possible. Remove the cut nails from the planks so they don’t scratch the siding during handling, and label the planks so you can reinstall them in the same locations.

After you make your wall repair, install a new piece of water-resistive barrier (WRB) taped along its perimeter to the existing WRB and tuck its top under the existing WRB to shed water. Then reinstall the planks in reverse sequence. I install new nails in the old holes, using ring-shank nails with a slightly larger diameter than the originals for a secure grip. At the ends of planks where they slide beneath an overlying course, you’ll have to face-nail. Make sure the nail penetrates through the overlap at the underlying and overlying planks near where the blind nail used to be.

Sources indicate that work your way up the wall until you reach the last plank that will slip beneath the existing plank at the top of the repaired area, then face-nail the last reinstalled plank. Face nails can be left exposed and touched up with color-matching paint, but they will be noticeable compared to the blind-nailed siding on the rest of the wall. You can somewhat hide the heads by countersinking them: Make recesses with a drill-mounted countersink and then putty and paint the heads so they’re less obvious. Don’t try hammering the nail heads below the siding surface because you’ll break the fiber cement and the nails won’t hold well.

#102164. Tech Report: Air Barrier for an Elevated Home

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (598 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Finehomebuilding ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Air Barrier for an Elevated Home

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (598 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Finehomebuilding

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’m about to build a house on the coast in Charleston, S.C.
  • It’s wise to consider inward vapor drive in humid climates like Charleston.
  • There are a few ways to prevent this.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’m about to build a house on the coast in Charleston, S.C. (Climate Zone 3A). It’s elevated on wood pilings and the space under the house is open to the outdoors, enclosed only with louvered panels between the pilings. I have most of the enclosure details nailed down, but I haven’t determined the best way to air-seal and insulate the open floor trusses above the pilings. My biggest concern is hot, humid air from below reaching the underside of the air-conditioned subfloor and condensing on the surface. What’s the best strategy to insulate and air-seal the underside of an elevated coastal home?

It’s wise to consider inward vapor drive in humid climates like Charleston. When the outdoor dew point is higher than the air-conditioned indoor temperature, there’s going to be a strong moisture drive from the outside toward the home’s interior, which allows water to accumulate in the materials below the flooring. Prolonged wetting can lead to rotted framing, mold problems, and damaged flooring, along with damage to other materials in contact with the floor.

There are a few ways to prevent this. One option is to place a vapor-retarding insulation layer—spray foam—right below the subfloor. The outside (bottom) of the foam will be close enough to the outdoor temperature that water won’t condense on the surface, and the foam will substantially block moisture from moving through it. Provided no ductwork is run in the floor, it’s a way to get decent air-sealing, and the cost is reasonable as well.

Sources indicate that that said, I don’t like to use spray foam across an entire floor—it’s risky to install and full of questionable chemicals. Another option is to create a conditioned space within the floor system. The challenge is air-sealing around the posts, beams, and structural hardware that hold up the house and the plumbing and electrical lines in this area. Plus, you’ll have to condition the space, which requires additional HVAC work. This can be simple (like adding a supply register and a path back to the house) or pretty involved (running ductwork down walls to reach the underfloor space).

My third and preferred option is to create an airtight, vapor-retarding layer across the bottom of the floor trusses. A layer of XPS or foil-faced polyiso (don’t use EPS, it’s too vapor-open) across the bottom of the whole floor will help slow vapor drive into the floor system and bring practical benefits like easier air-sealing and a little additional insulation. In Climate Zone 3A, turn to the International Residential Code (IRC) Table 806.5 in the section on roof ventilation for guidance on the R-value needed, since the floor system will have insulation levels comparable to roofs. The table calls for 1/2 in. of rigid insulation. Using the calculation procedure in the table footnotes indicates a higher level (in the 11/2-in. range) might be less risky, assuming you are completely filling a 12-in. to 16-in. floor-truss cavity with blown-in cellulose or fiberglass, which will be more than the code-required R-38 when the table was developed. Cover the foam board with fiberglass-faced drywall sheathing or plywood. Air-­sealing will still be complex given the elevated construction, and attention will need to be paid to the rim joist/perimeter (spray foam works in this area, as shown in the drawing). But, this system would really slow vapor movement throughout the floor system.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Artem Stryzhak, 36, a Ukrainian national, was sentenced today to 70 months in prison for conspiracy to commit computer fraud in connection with a series of ransomware attacks that targeted hospitals, government entities, law firms, and other businesses around the world.

Industry observers note that “This sentence concludes a years-long, multi-continent investigation into a defendant who participated in cyber-attacks against Americans’ businesses and health care,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “Cybercriminals who terrorize American businesses cannot evade justice by operating from abroad or hiding behind sophisticated technology. Artem Stryzhak’s sentence underscores the Justice Department’s resolve to dismantle ransomware groups, hold them accountable, and protect American businesses and people from cyber extortion.”.

It has been revealed that “Ransomware attacks like those committed by the defendant wreak enormous havoc — harming victim companies that pay millions in remediation and ransoms, preventing hospitals and other critical facilities from accessing data, and putting sensitive information in the hands of bad actors,” said U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. for the Eastern District of Upcoming York. “Today’s sentence reflects that cybercriminals cannot hide from law enforcement and will face significant punishment for their criminal conduct. We remain determined to capture Volodymyr Tymoshchuk, a serial ransomware developer and Stryzhak’s co-conspirator.”.

“Disrupting a ransomware group that attacked approximately 1,500 victims worldwide and sentencing a defendant who had targeted healthcare during the COVID-19 pandemic is of significant importance to this office,” mentioned U.S. Attorney Gregory W. Kehoe for the Middle District of Florida. “We are proud of our law enforcement partners for their skilled investigative work in bringing this criminal to justice.”.

“Artem Stryzhak is a prolific cybercriminal who worked with multiple ransomware groups to target U.S. businesses and hospitals,” noted Operations Director Brett Leatherman of the FBI’s Cyber Branch. “These groups disrupted patient care and caused more than $100 million in losses. Today’s sentence reflects the seriousness of Stryzhak’s crimes and demonstrates the FBI’s global reach and extensive network of international partners. Multiple field offices contributed to this investigation, and our work does not end here. We will continue to leverage every tool at our disposal to track down Stryzhak’s co-conspirators and hold them accountable, including Volodymyr Viktorovych Tymoshchuk.”.

Sources indicate that according to court documents, Stryzhak, formerly of Barcelona, Spain, conspired with others to perpetrate ransomware attacks on behalf of multiple ransomware groups against victim computer networks in the United States and other countries. The conspiracies caused significant damage to victim computer systems. Beginning in approximately June 2021, Stryzhak joined the ongoing Nefilim conspiracy as a Nefilim ransomware affiliate. Stryzhak was given access to the Nefilim ransomware and agreed with one of the Nefilim ransomware group administrators, Volodymyr Tymoshchuk, to pay the Nefilim administrators, including Tymoshchuk, 20% of the ransom proceeds extorted from victims in exchange for Stryzhak’s access to the Nefilim ransomware.

The ransomware attacks that Stryzhak conducted with Nefilim ransomware included a June 2021 attack in which Stryzhak stole data from a manufacturer in the oil and gas transportation industry. About a week later, Stryzhak created email addresses that were incorporated in a ransom note sent to the victim company. Stryzhak conspired with the Nefilim ransomware actors until at least October 2021. If a victim paid the ransom demand, the perpetrators provided the decryption key, enabling the victim to decrypt files locked by the ransomware.

According to recent reports, also according to court documents, Stryzhak separately joined the Hive ransomware group as one of its earliest affiliates. From June 2021 to January 2023, Hive conspirators attacked approximately 1,500 victims worldwide, including government entities, hospitals, and businesses. Hive ransomware attacks caused major disruptions in victim daily operations around the world and affected responses to the COVID-19 pandemic. In one case, a hospital attacked by the Hive ransomware group had to forgo digital technology to treat existing patients and was unable to accept new patients immediately following the attack.

In his role as a Hive affiliate, Stryzhak and his co-conspirators deployed Hive ransomware against seven victims, including law firms, a dentist office, and a healthcare provider during the COVID-19 pandemic. Victims were unable to access their encrypted data. The FBI, as part of a months-long disruption campaign against the Hive ransomware group, provided a decryption key to one of Stryzhak’s victims, thereby allowing that victim to decrypt its encrypted data without having to pay a ransom.

Stryzhak was arrested in Spain in June 2024 and extradited to the United States in April 2025. Stryzhak pleaded guilty in December 2025 to two counts of conspiracy to commit fraud, extortion, and related activity in connection with computers.

The FBI Springfield Field Office investigated the Nefilim ransomware case and the FBI Tampa Field Office investigated the Hive ransomware case. The Criminal Division’s Office of International Affairs, the FBI’s New York Field Office, and Spanish law enforcement authorities provided substantial assistance locating, arresting, and extraditing Stryzhak.

Sources indicate that acting Assistant Deputy Chief James S. Yoon of the Criminal Division’s Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section (CCIPS), former CCIPS Senior Trial Attorney Brian Z. Mund, and Assistant United States Attorneys Alexander F. Mindlin and Ellen H. Sise of the Eastern District of Upcoming York’s National Security and Cybercrime Section prosecuted the Nefilim ransomware case. CCIPS Trial Attorneys Alison M. Zitron and Christen M. Gallagher and Assistant United States Attorney Hannah Watson of the Middle District of Florida prosecuted the Hive ransomware case.

Recent findings suggest that the U.S. Department of State’s Transnational Organized Crime (TOC) Rewards Program has offered a reward of up to $11 million for information leading to the arrest and/or conviction or location of Stryzhak’s charged co-conspirator, Volodymyr Tymoshchuk. Anyone with information about Tymoshchuk should contact the FBI via phone at +1-917-242-1407, by email at TymoTips@fbi.gov, by contacting your local field office, if in the United States, or by contacting the nearest U.S. Embassy, if located overseas. More information about the Tymoshchuk TOC reward offer and one related to Hive ransomware is located on the State Department website.

It has been revealed that CCIPS investigates and prosecutes cybercrime and intellectual property (IP) crime in coordination with domestic and international law enforcement agencies, often with assistance from the private sector. Since 2020, CCIPS has secured the conviction of over 180 cyber and IP criminals, and court orders for the return of over $350 million in victim funds.

#102161. Latest Update: Israeli-American Emory Professor's Defamation Case Against CAIR Georgia and Emory Student Can Go Forward (in Part)

Latest Update: Israeli-American Emory Professor's Defamation Case Against CAIR Georgia and Emory Student Can Go Forward (in Part)

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2460 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that some excerpts from the long opinion by Judge Thomas Thrash (N.D.
  • Sources indicate that this action arises out of alleged defamatory statements that Defendant Umaymah Mohammad, a student at the Emory University School of Medicine, made about Plaintiff Joshua Winer, a physician and professor at Emory.
  • In a recent development, nearly two months later, in March 2024, the Plaintiff published an op-ed piece in an Israeli news publication sharing his decision to travel to Israel to volunteer as a physician in the Israeli Defense Force ("IDF") following the October 7th Hamas attack on Israel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that some excerpts from the long opinion by Judge Thomas Thrash (N.D. Ga.) yesterday in Winer v. Mohammad:.

Sources indicate that this action arises out of alleged defamatory statements that Defendant Umaymah Mohammad, a student at the Emory University School of Medicine, made about Plaintiff Joshua Winer, a physician and professor at Emory. Mohammad, who is Palestinian, sent an email to the entire School of Medicine student and faculty body on January 17, 2024, in which the Plaintiff alleges she "praised terrorism against Israel, expressed her hatred towards Israel and the United States, and stated that Israel, the United States, and Emory are perpetrating a genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.".

In a recent development, nearly two months later, in March 2024, the Plaintiff published an op-ed piece in an Israeli news publication sharing his decision to travel to Israel to volunteer as a physician in the Israeli Defense Force ("IDF") following the October 7th Hamas attack on Israel. The Plaintiff identifies as Jewish and maintains dual American and Israeli citizenship. He is a surgical oncologist at Emory Winship Cancer Institute, a professor in the Department of Surgery, Division of Surgical Oncology at the School of Medicine, and serves as the School of Medicine Surgical Clerkship Director.

It has been revealed that in April 2024, Mohammad participated in an interview for a news organization called Democracy Now!. In the interview, Mohammad was asked about the email she sent and was asked to explain the importance of the matter to her. As part of her response, Mohammad referenced Winer by stating that.

one of the professors of medicine we have at Emory recently went to serve as a volunteer medic in the Israeli Offense Force [sic] and recently came back. This man participated in aiding and abetting a genocide, in aiding and abetting the destruction of the healthcare system in Gaza and the murder of over 400 healthcare workers, and is now back at Emory so-called teaching medical students and residents how to take care of patients.

Industry observers note that mohammad was ultimately suspended from the School of Medicine for one year based on her comments in the Democracy Now! interview. In November 2024, Mohammad participated in a podcast hosted by the International Union of Scientists in which she made similar statements about the Plaintiff. In January 2025, she made more statements about the Plaintiff's IDF service in the online publication Mondoweiss. In the Mondoweiss piece, Mohammad claimed that the Plaintiff "believe[d] in the legitimacy of apartheid, and that some human lives are not as notable as others.".

At the end of the piece, she provided a link to a social media post by Defendants National Students for Justice in Palestine ("NSJP") and Doctors Against Genocide ("DAG"), which ultimately led to a campaign on the website of Action Network that "contained additional false statements about Plaintiff and identified him by name." NSJP and DAG also published posts on Instagram regarding the Action Network campaign, which directly quoted Mohammad's Democracy Now! interview. These Defendants made a second Instagram post a few weeks later. The Plaintiff alleges that Defendant WESPAC is NSJP's fiscal sponsor and, therefore, "knowingly funded and facilitated NSJP's coordinated efforts to vilify Plaintiff and pressure Emory to discipline [him].".

In February 2025, Defendant CAIR Georgia held a press conference on the subject of Mohammad's suspension, during which she made the following statement:.

[Emory] disciplined me for exposing Emory's complicity in the destruction of Gaza in an interview where I mentioned an unnamed physician who served in the military, actively engaged in the genocidal campaign against the Palestinian people, my people … I cannot learn from a physician who might have fired one of the 355 bullets that landed in 6 year old Hind Rajab's body. Or who might have helped make the decision to bomb one of the hospitals in Gaza. Or who might have celebrated the murder of our communities on the rubble still wet with Palestinian blood. A doctor who cannot see Palestinians as human beings will return to Atlanta to offer the same disposability to black and brown patients at home.

CAIR Georgia, along with CAIR Foundation Inc. ("CAIR Foundation"), also issued a press release with a link to Mohammad's Democracy Now! interview and rebroadcasted this speech on its Instagram account on February 11, 2025. In this post, (the "IG Post"), CAIR Georgia also replied to comments by providing a link to a previously circulated email template and phone script that identified the Plaintiff by name and called for Emory to investigate him and/or terminate his employment.

Mohammad's statements were later broadcasted and published by television stations and news outlets. Defendant Ibrahim Jouja was the President of Emory SJP when it shared NSJP and DAG's posts on the Emory SJP Instagram account, and also made or collaborated on similar posts sharing the Democracy Now! interview and identifying the Plaintiff "as a physician with military combat experience against Palestinians." Defendant Rupa Marya works with Mohammad as a cofounder of DAG and, the Plaintiff alleges, she has "frequently identified Plaintiff by name and used her social media platforms to spread harmful and reputationally damaging statements about him," including blaming him for the termination of a Palestinian professor at Emory School of Medicine and accusing him of participating in a genocide….

The court allowed plaintiff's federal claim for conspiracy to interfere with civil rights (42 U.S.C. § 1985) to go forward:.

Section 1985(3) "created a cause of action against private individuals who, among other things, undertake conspiracies for the purpose of depriving, either directly or indirectly, any person or class of persons of the equal protection of the laws, or of equal privileges and immunities under the laws." "That § 1985(3) reaches private action does not, however, mean that it was intended to apply to all tortious, conspiratorial interferences with the rights of others." ….

The Plaintiff hinges [the remaining part of] his § 1985(3) claim on the alleged violations of his rights under … Title VI. The Eleventh Circuit does not appear to have addressed whether a violation of Title VI is enforceable against a private conspirator under § 1985(3), so for the reasons the Court expressed in its prior orders, the Court presumes that it is. To state a claim under § 1985(3), a plaintiff must establish that the defendant has.

(1) conspired or gone in disguise on the highway or on the premises of another, (2) for the purpose of depriving, either directly or indirectly, any person or class of persons of the equal protection of the laws, or of equal privileges and immunities under the laws, (3) taken or caused an action to be taken in furtherance of the conspiracy's object, and (4) injured an individual's person or property or deprived her of exercising any right or privilege of a United States citizen.

Title VI provides that no one shall "be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any program or activity receiving Federal financial assistance" on the ground of his "race, color, or national origin." To state a claim under § 2000d, a plaintiff must only allege that the defendant receives federal funds, that it discriminated against the plaintiff on the basis of race, color, or national origin, and that it did so in the course of a federally funded program….

[Plaintiff asserts] a § 1985(3) claim based on a conspiracy to induce Emory to violate his Title VI rights. And for purposes of a motion to a dismiss, he has stated such a claim as to the CAIR Foundation theory. The Plaintiff alleges that CAIR Foundation receives federal funding, making § 2000d enforceable against it. More specifically, he alleges that CAIR Foundation received federal funding, that it conspired with the other defendants, including Mohammad and Jouja, to subject him to discrimination based on his race and national origin by posting the IG Posts at issue, which he alleges were defamatory and filled with false accusations, and that this discrimination was carried out "in the administration of CAIR Foundation's program or activities receiving Federal financial assistance." The Plaintiff also identifies the specific actions he alleges the Defendants took in furtherance of the conspiracy, including the statements Mohammad made that Jouja is allegedly responsible for as president of Emory SJP. At this early stage, these allegations satisfy the elements of a § 1985(3) claim predicated on a Title VI violation.

Whether this claim can withstand summary judgment is a question for another day. Accordingly, the Defendants' Motion to Dismiss is denied as to this argument.

In the process, the court also held that plaintiff had adequately alleged the "protected class" element of § 1985(3), by alleging that he was targeted for his national origin:.

Industry observers note that the Defendants next argue that the Plaintiff unfairly conflates anti-Zionism with antisemitism in order to "place an entire area of First Amendment-protected political, legal and ethical discussion off limits." … The Defendants essentially argue that because Zionism is (in their view) solely a political philosophy, the Plaintiff has actually alleged that their actions were not truly motivated by his Jewish identity but instead by their opposition to Zionism and serving in the IDF. But taking that view would require the Court to construe the Plaintiff's allegations narrowly and in their favor, which it cannot do at this stage.

What the Plaintiff actually alleges, if construed in his favor—and what the Court must accept as true at this stage—is that his military service resulted from a "sense of duty to serve the Jewish homeland, which is integral to his racial identity as a Jew" ["racial" is here used in the historical sense that included what we would now call "ethnicity," consistent with the Court's caselaw on § 1985 and related statutes -EV] and that his association with Zionism is also "an integral part of Jewish identity for a very significant number of Jews." In essence, the Plaintiff alleges that his military service and association with Zionism are markers of his own personal Jewish identity, and that his Jewish heritage as an Israeli national is a protected class.

Recent findings suggest that critical to this interpretation is the Plaintiff's allegations that his IDF service was tied to the duty he felt based on his nationality and the significance of Zionism in Jewish culture. These allegations suffice at this stage to demonstrate that a discriminatory animus based on a protected class—the Plaintiff's national origin—motivated the Defendants' actions, not mere political differences.

Sources indicate that and the court concluded that plaintiff had adequately alleged that defendants' speech fell within the First Amendment exception for defamation. It concluded that plaintiff had adequately alleged that he wasn't a limited purpose public figure, despite his op-ed. And the court concluded that plaintiff had adequately alleged that the statements about him contained false factual assertions:.

Plaintiff asserts that parts of Mohammad's statement in the Democracy Now! interview are demonstrably false, including her statements that the Plaintiff "aid[ed and abett[ed] a genocide" and "aid[ed] and abett[ed] the destruction of the healthcare system in Gaza." Regardless of whether these statements express political opinion, the statements could reasonably "imply defamatory facts about the plaintiff that are capable of being proved false" when the facts are construed in the Plaintiff's favor[.] This is because Mohammad's statements—that the Plaintiff alleges Jouja is responsible for reposting as president of Emory SJP, along with supportive commentary—imply that the Plaintiff actively participated in combat operations during his service in the IDF, but the Plaintiff pled that he served.

In a recent development, solely in his capacity as a physician, providing medical care to wounded soldiers. His involvement in combat was limited to situations in which his unit came under direct attack … Mohammad had no factual basis to claim that Plaintiff participated in or approved the bombing of hospitals in Gaza [or] celebrated the killing of Palestinians.

According to recent reports, the Court agrees with the Defendants' position that characterizing the Israel-Hamas war as a genocide is likely an inactionable opinion because it reflects a "subjective assessment, as to which reasonable minds could differ, [and which] cannot be proved false." But the statements at glitch here go further and allege personal combat participation in the alleged genocide—a fact which the Plaintiff could prove at a later stage is false. At this stage, his allegations about his role are enough to satisfy the "false and defamatory statement" element of his defamation per se claim and the falsity element of his false light claim.

The same is true of part of Mohammad's statement during the press conference, in which she stated that.

In a recent development, [h]aving a physician faculty member who participated in a military convicted of committing genocide against Palestinians makes me feel unsafe. It makes black and brown medical students feel unsafe. It makes black and brown and indigenous patients feel unsafe. I cannot learn from a physician who might have fired one of the 355 bullets that landed in 6 year old Hind Rajab's body. Or who might have helped make the decision to bomb one of the hospitals in Gaza … a doctor who cannot see Palestinians as human beings will return to Atlanta to offer the same disposability to black and brown patients at home.

Industry observers note that there are parts of the statement that express Mohammad's opinion, such as the part that the Plaintiff's military service makes her, and "black and brown medical students," feel unsafe. This is a subjective assessment that cannot be proved false, so this part of the statement is not actionable. But the part of the statement that suggests the Plaintiff might have been involved in combat decisions or actions and accuses him of not "see[ing] Palestinians as human beings" and offering "the same disposability to black and brown patients" at Emory certainly implies that the Plaintiff engaged in combat operations while serving in the IDF and that patients of certain races are therefore not safe in his care.

The same is true of the statement in Emory SJP's March 28, 2025 collaborative IG Post that described the Plaintiff as "a physician with military combat experience against Palestinians." The Plaintiff has alleged counter-facts that, if accepted as true, prove these portions of the statements false, so the Plaintiff states a claim as to these portions of the press conference statement and the March 28 Emory SJP IG Post.

According to recent reports, for these reasons, the Court will dismiss the portion of the Plaintiff's defamation and false light claims predicated on the opinion portions of the statements identified above. The Court will deny the Defendants' Motion to Dismiss as to the remainder of their First Amendment and opinion-based arguments….

#102160. Finding the Right Clients

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2381 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Finehomebuilding ↗ Open Full Page

Finding the Right Clients

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2381 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Finehomebuilding

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that I spend a lot of time talking with builders who tell me they don’t really do marketing.
  • My first response is usually that this is a good thing.
  • But I have also seen construction companies reach a point where the business landscape has changed, and reputation alone is not leading to the right clients.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that I spend a lot of time talking with builders who tell me they don’t really do marketing. Usually they say it with pride: “We’ve never had to. All of our work comes from word of mouth.”.

My first response is usually that this is a good thing. If you’ve spent years building a organization where past clients, architects, and trade partners keep sending work your way, you’ve built something valuable. In construction, reputation matters, and that kind of trust is earned over time. I would never tell a builder to replace that with advertising.

But I have also seen construction companies reach a point where the business landscape has changed, and reputation alone is not leading to the right clients. Good builders often struggle because the right people don’t know they exist.

According to recent reports, the phone may still be ringing, but the work coming in doesn’t always match where the manufacturer wants to go next. The business has evolved, but what people know about it hasn’t necessarily evolved with it.

Industry observers note that those are the moments when someone usually states, often a little reluctantly, “I guess we need to do some marketing.” That may indeed be the case. But I think there is a simpler and more useful way to frame the problem: Are you known for the work you actually want to do? That is where I would start.

Industry observers note that I’ve spent more than 20 years helping businesses and organizations grow, evolve, and connect with the people they want to reach, from owning and running a design and marketing agency to leading a destination marketing organization and working across marketing, branding, organizational leadership, consulting, and coaching. Today, as director of marketing and a business consultant with HELM Construction Solutions, I bring those experiences together in my work with builders, helping them think about where their business is going, the work they want more of, and what makes them different.

It has been revealed that sit across the table with an experienced builder and you quickly understand what makes them different. But if you haven’t had that conversation, how would you know? I see this all the time: Some of the most valuable things about a construction tech giant live almost entirely in the owner’s head. The challenge is making more of that knowledge visible.

Before I talk with a builder about websites, social media, advertising, or anything else that might get labeled “marketing,” I want to understand the business they are trying to build. What kind of work would they happily do again? Which projects are profitable? Which projects make the crew proud? Which clients trust the process? Where do they want to work? Who do they want to work alongside? What do they want the organization to look like in five years? And—just as crucial—what do they want less of?

In a recent development, that last question can be surprisingly provocative. Construction companies are often encouraged to think about growth only in terms of more: more projects, more employees, more revenue, more leads. But growth doesn’t always mean more projects. Sometimes it means being more intentional about the work you take on.

I’ll ask why a builder does something a certain way, and suddenly we’re deep into a story about a detail, a process, or a hard-earned lesson that changed how they work. Those stories are usually where the good stuff is, and where what makes a organization different becomes clear.

At this point, a lot of decisions get easier. You don’t need to reach everybody. You just need to become more visible to the people who value that kind of work.

If you aren’t sure how to identify the right types of projects for your business, I often suggest looking backward before looking forward. Choose three to five projects from the last few years that you would happily do again. Think about the jobs where the fit was right—the client trusted you, the work suited the strengths of your crew, the project was financially healthy, and the architect or designer was collaborative. Problems came up, as they always do, but the team solved them together rather than turning on one another. When the project ended, you were proud not only of what you built but of how you built it.

Sources indicate that then ask a simple question: How did that project find us? You may discover that the same architect appears several times. Maybe a handful of past clients have been quietly sending people your way for years. Perhaps one designer, Realtor, supplier, or fellow builder keeps connecting you to projects that are an unusually good fit. Those patterns matter. They show you where to focus your time and attention. And when you’re trying to become known somewhere latest, that kind of focus becomes even more crucial.

For example, Sycamore Builders in western North Carolina has strong experience with architect-led custom homes in mountain communities. But as the tech giant looks to expand into nearby markets, it faces a familiar challenge: Reputation is local.

It has been revealed that in some of those communities, builders have been around for generations. Their trucks are familiar. Realtors and architects know them. Their projects are part of the landscape. That familiarity has been built over years. You cannot advertise your way into a 25-year relationship.

So Sycamore is taking a patient approach by building relationships with architects and Realtors, sharing more of the stories behind its work, and showing up consistently in a few specific communities. The goal isn’t a flood of calls. One or two well-aligned upcoming builds a year can make a ­meaningful difference.

If the word marketing makes you want to stop reading, forget about marketing for a minute. Take an hour with your business partner, project manager, or someone who knows your tech giant well and work through these questions. Let your answers guide you in pinpointing the type of work you want to find. Once you do, you won’t need to network every week, post every day, or constantly update your website. Pick a few actions that fit your business, and keep doing them.

What work do people call you for—and what work do you wish people called you for?

Recent findings suggest that be honest with yourself. Is the work you’re doing now the work you want to be doing? If not, that’s your starting point.

What are five projects you’d do again tomorrow?

What made those projects good for the client, the crew, and the business? Writing the answers down can help you determine the type of work you want to do more of.

How did each of those projects find you?

Maybe it was a past client, an architect, a builder, a Realtor, a jobsite sign, a Google search, or something else. Don’t guess—find out. Then you can use those same methods to find similar projects in the future.

Who is connected to the work you want?

It has been revealed that make a list of the Realtors, architects, designers, and trade partners who are connected to the kinds of projects and clients you want more of, using your favorite projects as a guide. Who do you already know? Who consistently connects you to good-fit work? Who would you like to build a stronger relationship with?

How can you stay connected to those people?

According to recent reports, could you invite someone to a jobsite, meet for coffee, share an interesting project over email, attend an industry event, or simply check in occasionally? Staying in touch helps potential partners remember you and your business when the right project comes along.

When someone looks you up, can they see what you want to be known for?

Do your website and social media show the types of projects you want to do? Are you telling the stories behind that work and making your expertise visible? The clearer you are about the work you want, the easier it is for the right clients and partners to recognize that you’re the right fit.

In a recent development, this is usually the point where someone states, “Carrie, I have houses to build. I can’t spend all my time updating a website, posting on social media, meeting architects for coffee, and telling project stories.”.

That’s fair, and I don’t want you to. Go back to what you learned about your best projects, and choose two or three things you can realistically keep doing to continue getting this sort of work. For example, maybe that means staying connected to a small group of architects and adding a strong project story to your website every few months.

Sources indicate that then pay attention to what happens. Ask every upcoming caller how they heard about you, notice which relationships lead to good-fit projects, and see whether the work coming through the door starts to look more like the work you want.

Recent findings suggest that for example, longtime high-performance builder Steve DeMetrick of DeMetrick Housewrights has spent more than two decades developing a reputation for building homes that demonstrate thoughtful craftsmanship, durability, and energy-efficiency. Most of his work has come through referrals. He has deep expertise, strong relationships, and plenty of experience. He is not trying to make the phone ring more.

Sources indicate that in fact, when we started talking about where he wants the firm to go next, his answer was almost the opposite of what we typically associate with growth. He wants to slow down. He wants fewer projects at a time, larger scope, deeper involvement with each client, earlier collaboration with architects, and more opportunity to use the knowledge he has accumulated over decades.

The more we talked, the clearer it became that high-performance construction is only part of what makes his company valuable. What really stands out is how he approaches the whole process—bringing design, budget, and scope together early and getting everyone working together sooner. That can lead to better decisions, fewer surprises, and a better experience for everyone involved. But that type of value is a lot harder to advertise on the side of a truck.

Sources indicate that the goal isn’t simply to tell more people that DeMetrick Housewrights builds high-performance homes. It is to make more of Steve’s thinking visible, to tell the stories behind projects, to explain why he approaches preconstruction the way he does, and to give potential clients and collaborators a better sense of what it is actually like to work with him. The point isn’t to create content for the sake of content. It is to help people see expertise that is already there.

I’ve seen the same thing with Bell Street Builders in Maine, an employee-owned cooperative that does thoughtful restoration and renovation work around Portland and Casco Bay, including historic homes, architect-driven projects, and coastal and island construction. Those projects come with the kinds of challenges experienced builders know well: older structures that reveal surprises, coastal exposure, difficult logistics, complicated sequencing, and the need to make decisions carefully when clients may be living elsewhere.

When I worked on Bell Street’s strategic direction, one theme kept reappearing: Bell Street knows old buildings. This is much more useful than generically saying the company does “quality construction.”.

Sources indicate that if you own a 100-year-old house in Portland and are about to open walls that may be hiding decades of issues, you want a builder who understands what they’re looking at and can respond without turning every surprise into a crisis. If you’re an architect working on that house, you want a builder who can solve problems collaboratively and respect the building while still moving the project forward.

Bell Street did not need to become known to every homeowner in southern Maine. The better opportunity was to become more recognizable for the work the manufacturer does best and in the places where it wants to do more of it. That meant making sure its website and social channels showed more of its historic work and the stories behind complex projects, staying connected with architects and designers who work on those kinds of homes, and building relationships in priority communities such as Portland’s West End, Foreside communities, and the Casco Bay islands.

Becoming recognizable doesn’t have to mean constantly creating something newly introduced. One good project can go a long way. Document the challenges during construction, photograph the finished work, explain what the team had to solve, and share that story on a website, social media, or directly with architects and past clients who may know someone planning a similar project.

Industry observers note that I genuinely appreciate builders’ resistance to marketing. It usually stems from a belief that the work should matter most. I think so too.

In a recent development, A clever website cannot make up for poor craftsmanship. Advertising cannot replace trust, and social media cannot substitute for treating clients well, running a good jobsite, respecting trade partners, or standing behind what you build. Your reputation still has to be earned.

Once you’ve earned it, however, there is nothing wrong with helping it travel. That doesn’t require becoming a marketer. It simply means being a little more intentional about making the work, knowledge, and people behind your firm visible.

Recent findings suggest that and there is a benefit beyond finding the kinds of projects you want. The same things that help clients, architects, designers, and trade partners understand your manufacturer also help potential employees understand it. Most builder websites show houses, but far fewer show the people behind them. A good carpenter who is considering their next move may want to know what kinds of projects they would work on, who they would work alongside, whether people stay, and whether there is room to grow.

According to recent reports, make it easier for future employees and clients alike to understand who you are, what you do well, and where you’re headed. Because good work will lead to more good work, but only if people know about it.
